title: What psychology is
description: Psychology, named from Greek words for "soul" and "study of", is today the scientific study of the mind and behavior.

facts.text: The word psychology comes from Greek psykhe, meaning "breath, spirit, soul", plus -logia, meaning "study of".
Psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behavior.

title: Measuring a mind you cannot see
description: Because no one can read minds directly, psychologists test ideas by measuring things they can observe (behavior, biological signals and what people report) and publishing results so others can repeat them.

facts.text: Scientists test only what can be perceived and measured: the idea that a bird sings because it is happy cannot be tested, since there is no way to measure a bird's happiness, but people can be asked why they sing.

Because no one can read another person's mind, psychologists study mental processes indirectly by measuring observable behavior, biological indicators and self-reports, and draw inferences about the mind from them.
Psychologists test a hypothesis by observation or experiment and then publish or present the results so that others can replicate or build on them.

title: The main areas of psychology
description: Psychology splits into areas such as biopsychology, cognitive, developmental, social and personality psychology, organized in the APA into 54 divisions.

facts.text: Biopsychology studies how the nervous system relates to behavior, and cognitive psychology studies thoughts and how they relate to experience and action.

Developmental psychology studies change across the lifespan, social psychology studies how people interact with and relate to others, and personality psychology studies the patterns of thought and behavior that make each person unique.
The American Psychological Association (APA), the largest organization of psychologists in the world, has 54 divisions representing specialties within psychology.

title: Psychologists, psychiatrists and counselors
description: Psychologists hold a doctorate and assess and treat with therapy and testing; psychiatrists are medical doctors who can prescribe; counselors and therapists usually hold a master's degree.

facts.text: Clinical psychology receives the most attention in popular media, and many people mistakenly assume that all psychology is clinical psychology.
In the United States, psychologists who treat people hold a doctoral degree (a PhD or a PsyD); they assess people with interviews and psychological tests, make diagnoses and provide therapy.
Psychiatrists are medical doctors (MD or DO) who have completed training in psychiatry; because of that medical training they can prescribe medication, and they can also diagnose and provide therapy.
Counselors and therapists usually hold a master's degree in a mental health field and are licensed under titles such as Licensed Professional Counselor.
Only people who pass a licensure exam, after meeting state requirements, can call themselves licensed clinical or counseling psychologists.

title: Where psychologists work
description: Psychologists work in clinical and counseling practice, schools, courts, workplaces and university research.

facts.text: Clinical psychology focuses on diagnosing and treating psychological disorders, while counseling psychology focuses on emotional, social, vocational and health outcomes in people considered psychologically healthy.
Forensic psychologists work within the justice system, for example assessing whether a person is competent to stand trial and advising on eyewitness testimony.
Industrial-organizational psychologists apply psychology in workplaces, school psychologists work in education, and many psychologists with a PhD teach and do research at universities.

title: Wundt's first psychology laboratory
description: In 1879 Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory, at Leipzig, bringing experiments and measurement such as reaction times to questions that had belonged to philosophy.

facts.text: Wilhelm Wundt, a German scientist with a medical degree who taught physiology, established the first psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig in 1879.
Until Wundt, psychology had been regarded as a branch of philosophy; he stressed experimental methods drawn from the natural sciences.
In Wundt's laboratory, a participant received a stimulus such as a light, image or sound and pressed a button, and an apparatus recorded the reaction time to one-thousandth of a second.

title: Introspection
description: Wundt used trained introspection, people examining their own conscious experience, but reports stayed subjective and observers often disagreed.

facts.text: Wundt used introspection, in which a trained person examines their own conscious experience as objectively as possible, aiming to find the components of consciousness.
Despite training, introspection remained highly subjective, and there was very little agreement between individuals.

title: Freud's unconscious mind
description: Sigmund Freud, a medical doctor, pictured most of the mind as an unconscious store of hidden feelings and urges, reached through dreams, free association and slips of the tongue.

facts.text: Sigmund Freud was an Austrian neurologist, a medical doctor rather than a psychologist.
Freud compared the mind to an iceberg, saying that only about one-tenth of it is conscious and the rest is unconscious.

Freud saw the unconscious mind as a store of feelings and urges we are not aware of, which he believed could be reached through dream analysis, the first words that come to mind and slips of the tongue.
Psychoanalysis, in which a patient talks about their experiences, was popularized by Freud and is still used today.

title: What Freud got wrong and right
description: Freud treated his own interpretations as proof, and most of his specific ideas, like his childhood stages, found no research support, while the broad idea that much of mental life is unconscious did.

facts.text: Freud treated his own recollections and his interpretations of patients' experiences and dreams as sufficient proof that his stages of childhood development were universal.
Most of Freud's specific ideas, such as his stages of childhood development, have not found support in modern research.

In a 1998 review, the psychologist Drew Westen found that a large body of research supports Freud's broad ideas that much of mental life is unconscious and that childhood experience helps shape personality.

title: Behaviorism
description: John Watson's behaviorism (1913) set aside introspection and the mind to study only observable behavior, aiming to predict and control it, and dominated American psychology for decades.

facts.text: In a 1913 paper, John B. Watson wrote that psychology as the behaviorist views it is a purely objective, experimental branch of natural science whose goal is the prediction and control of behavior, and that introspection forms no essential part of its methods.
Watson believed objective analysis of the mind was impossible, so he focused directly on observable behavior; this approach became known as behaviorism.
Behaviorism dominated experimental psychology for several decades; especially in North America, it dominated through the 1950s.
Behaviorism's objective methods, especially experiments, helped establish psychology as a science, and its ideas are still used in behavioral therapy and classrooms.

title: Skinner and consequences
description: B. F. Skinner studied how consequences (reinforcement and punishment) change behavior, often using animals in a chamber of his design.

facts.text: B. F. Skinner, like Watson a behaviorist, concentrated on how behavior is affected by its consequences, treating reinforcement and punishment as major drivers of behavior.
Behaviorists commonly experimented on animals, such as rats in a Skinner box, assuming that what they learned could to some degree apply to human behavior.

title: The cognitive revolution
description: From the 1950s, linguistics, neuroscience and computer science brought the mind back into psychology, which began modeling it as an information processor; Neisser's 1967 textbook named the field.

facts.text: By the 1950s, new work in linguistics, neuroscience and computer science revived interest in the mind as a subject of science, a shift known as the cognitive revolution.

Around 1956, computers had existed for only a few years, and pioneers were founding artificial intelligence; most cognitive science since assumes the mind has representations like computer data structures and procedures like algorithms.
In 1967, Ulric Neisser published the first textbook titled Cognitive Psychology.

title: Chomsky's challenge to behaviorism
description: In 1959 Noam Chomsky argued that behaviorism could not explain how children learn language, since they understand and produce sentences they have never heard.

facts.text: In 1959, the linguist Noam Chomsky published a review of B. F. Skinner's book on verbal behavior arguing that behaviorist models cannot explain how young children learn language so quickly.
Chomsky pointed out that by age four or five children can understand and produce sentences they have never heard, and argued that language learning does not depend on detailed reinforcement.

title: Twin and adoption studies
description: Twin studies compare identical and fraternal twins, and adoption studies compare biological and adoptive relatives, to weigh genes against environment.

facts.text: Many questions psychologists would like to answer cannot be studied with experiments because of ethical concerns.
Twin studies compare how often a trait is shared by identical twins versus fraternal twins; adoption studies compare biological relatives with adoptive relatives.

Identical twins have almost no differences in their DNA, while fraternal twins share on average 50 percent of their DNA; if a trait is more similar in identical twins raised together than in fraternal twins, genes likely play a role.

title: What heritability means
description: Heritability estimates how much of the variation in a trait within one population comes from genetic differences; twin studies put the average near half, and it says nothing about one person or how changeable a trait is.

facts.text: A 2015 analysis by Tinca Polderman and colleagues of virtually all twin studies published over 50 years, covering 17,804 traits and about 14.5 million twin pairs, found an average heritability of 49 percent across all traits.

Heritability describes how much of the variation in a trait within a population is due to genetic differences; a heritability of 0.7 does not mean a trait is 70 percent caused by genes, and an estimate applies to one population in one environment.
Language spoken runs in families but has a heritability of zero because it is not under genetic control, while hair color is highly heritable yet easy to change with dye.

title: Case studies
description: A case study examines one person or a few people in depth: rich information, but hard to generalize because the cases are usually unusual.

facts.text: A case study focuses on one person or just a few individuals, and the richness of information it gathers is unmatched by any other single research method.
Case studies often focus on people with rare characteristics, so their findings can be hard to generalize to most other people.

title: Naturalistic observation
description: Researchers watch behavior in its natural setting while staying unnoticed, because people act less naturally when they know they are watched.

facts.text: Asked in class whether they always wash their hands after using the restroom, almost everyone may raise a hand, because many people are not comfortable answering such questions honestly.

Naturalistic observation means watching behavior in its natural setting, and observers stay inconspicuous because people who know they are being watched are less likely to behave naturally, as a driver followed by a police car might.
In 1960 Jane Goodall set up camp in the Gombe Stream reserve in Tanzania and began observing wild chimpanzees, a famous example of naturalistic observation.
Naturalistic observation gives realistic data, but researchers have no control over when, or whether, the behavior they want to see will happen.

title: Surveys and self-report
description: Surveys reach many people quickly but give less depth, and self-reports can be wrong because people lie, misremember or answer to look good.

facts.text: Surveys are lists of questions that make it easy to collect data from large numbers of people, but they cannot gather the same depth of information on each person as a case study.
People do not always answer surveys accurately: they may lie, misremember or answer in a way that makes them look good, for example reporting drinking less alcohol than they do.
Case studies, observation and surveys can find relationships between things, but only an experiment can show cause and effect.

title: Informed consent and debriefing
description: Before a study, participants learn what to expect, including risks, agree voluntarily and may quit at any time; if a study used deception, they get a full debriefing.

facts.text: An informed consent form describes what participants can expect, including risks; it makes clear that taking part is voluntary and can be stopped at any time without penalty, and that data stay confidential.
When participants are under 18, their parents or legal guardians must sign the informed consent form.
When a study uses deception, participants must receive a full debriefing at the end that honestly explains the study's purpose and why deception was needed.

title: Ethics review boards
description: In the United States, an institutional review board of scientists, administrators and community members must generally approve research on people before it starts.

facts.text: In the United States, any institution that receives federal support for research with people must have an institutional review board (IRB), a committee of scientists, administrators and community members that reviews study proposals; generally, a study needs its approval to go ahead.

title: Why research ethics rules exist
description: The Nuremberg Code (1947) and the exposure of the Tuskegee syphilis study (1972) led to the US National Research Act (1974) and the Belmont Report (1979).

facts.text: In 1947, the verdict in the trial of Nazi doctors who experimented on concentration camp prisoners set out ten points, known as the Nuremberg Code, starting with the rule that voluntary consent is absolutely essential.
In 1932, the US Public Health Service began a study of syphilis in 600 Black men in Alabama, 399 with the disease and 201 without, without collecting their informed consent.
The men with syphilis were never told they had it, and although penicillin became an effective treatment in the 1940s, they were not given it.
The Tuskegee study ended in 1972 after the press exposed it, and the outrage led directly to the National Research Act of 1974.
The Belmont Report of 1979, written by a commission created under the National Research Act, set out three principles for research on people: respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

title: From philosophy to science
description: Questions about the mind belonged to philosophy from Plato and Aristotle until the 19th century, when Wundt and James turned psychology into its own science.

facts.text: Attempts to understand the mind go back at least to ancient Greek philosophers such as Plato and Aristotle, and the study of mind remained part of philosophy until the nineteenth century, when experimental psychology developed.

Psychology became accepted as its own academic discipline in the late 1800s, and Wilhelm Wundt in Germany and William James in the United States are generally credited as its founders as a science separate from philosophy.

title: Sensation and transduction
description: Sensation happens when a sensory receptor detects a stimulus; the receptor turns the stimulus energy into nerve signals, a step called transduction.

facts.text: Sensory receptors are specialized neurons that respond to specific types of stimuli; when a receptor detects sensory information, sensation has occurred.
Light entering the eye causes changes in cells at the back of the eye, which relay messages to the central nervous system; converting stimulus energy into these nerve signals is called transduction.

title: Perception: making sense of sensation
description: Perception is how sensory information is organized, interpreted and consciously experienced; sensation is a physical process, perception a psychological one.

facts.text: Perception is the way sensory information is organized, interpreted and consciously experienced.
One way to put the difference: sensation is a physical process, whereas perception is psychological.
Smelling cinnamon rolls baking, the sensation is scent receptors detecting cinnamon, while the perception may be a memory of a grandmother's holiday baking.

title: Sensory adaptation
description: A stimulus that stays constant for a long time often stops being perceived even though receptors still sense it.

facts.text: People often stop perceiving stimuli that stay relatively constant for a long time, even though their receptors still sense them; this is sensory adaptation.
Although perceptions are built from sensations, not all sensations result in perception.
Sensory adaptation is why people stop feeling the weight of their clothing or hearing the hum of a projector in a lecture hall.

title: The just-noticeable difference
description: The just-noticeable difference, or difference threshold, is the smallest change between two stimuli a person detects half the time.

facts.text: The just noticeable difference, or difference threshold, is the smallest difference between two stimuli needed to tell them apart.
Because sensitivity varies through the day and with recent stimulation, the difference threshold is defined as the smallest difference detected 50 percent of the time.
A phone screen lighting up is noticed by many people in a dark movie theater but by very few in a brightly lit arena, though its brightness is the same.

title: Weber's law
description: The just-noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the starting stimulus, so bigger stimuli need bigger changes to be noticed. Ernst Weber described it in 1834.

facts.text: The German physiologist Ernst Heinrich Weber described the law in 1834, from research on lifting weights.
Telling a 1-pound object from a 2-pound one is easy, but telling 10 pounds from 11 pounds is much harder, though both differ by 1 pound.
Weber's law states that the just noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the original stimulus, so bigger stimuli need bigger changes to be noticed.
Weber's law has been shown not to hold at the extremes of stimulation.

title: Gestalt psychology
description: Max Wertheimer's 1912 study of apparent motion launched Gestalt psychology, which holds that the whole we perceive is different from the sum of its parts.

facts.text: In 1912 Max Wertheimer published a study of the phi phenomenon, in which still images shown in rapid succession appear to move; it marks the founding of Gestalt psychology.
Wertheimer and his colleagues Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka believed perception involves more than simply combining sensations, and founded Gestalt psychology.
The word gestalt means form or pattern, and Gestalt psychology holds that the whole is different from the sum of its parts.
Gestalt psychologists held that the brain creates perceptions in predictable ways and turned those ways into principles, which became extremely influential in perception research.

title: Gestalt grouping principles
description: Figure-ground, proximity, similarity, continuity and closure describe how the mind groups what it sees into objects.

facts.text: By the figure-ground principle, people divide a scene into a figure in focus and a background, which is why one image can be seen as a vase or as two faces.
By the principle of proximity, things close together are grouped; the spaces between words are what let us group letters into words.
By the principle of similarity, things that look alike are grouped, as when viewers group football players by the color of their uniforms.
By good continuation people see smooth, continuous lines rather than jagged, broken ones; by closure they see complete objects, such as a whole circle despite gaps.

title: Bottom-up and top-down processing
description: In bottom-up processing the stimulus drives perception; in top-down processing knowledge and expectations do. Perception uses both.

facts.text: In bottom-up processing, information from a stimulus drives perception; in top-down processing, knowledge and expectations drive it. Perception involves both.
A crash of dropped plates in a noisy restaurant captures attention bottom-up; searching for keys on a yellow fob only in likely places is a top-down search based on experience.
Many readers miss the repeated word in "Paris in the the spring" because they don't expect it; a beginning reader attending to each word is less likely to miss it.

title: Perceptual set
description: Perceptual hypotheses built from experience, expectations and personality form a perceptual set, a readiness to perceive things in a particular way.

facts.text: Perceptions rest on perceptual hypotheses, educated guesses informed by personality, experience and expectations, which together form a perceptual set.
Someone expecting an important phone call may think they hear the phone ringing in the shower when it isn't: motivation shifts what they detect.
Because perceptions are built from sensations but shaped by experiences and culture, they can be very different from person to person.

title: The McGurk effect
description: Pairing the sound "ba" with a face saying "ga" makes many people hear "da": the brain fuses what it sees and hears. How strongly people are fooled varies widely.

facts.text: Harry McGurk and John MacDonald reported the effect in Nature in 1976, in a paper titled "Hearing lips and seeing voices".
In the original report, 98 percent of adults heard "da" for one stimulus, an auditory "ba" paired with a video of lips saying "ga".
In the McGurk effect, pairing a speech sound with a mismatched mouth movement produces the perception of a third syllable, different from both.
Heard on its own without the video, the auditory syllable is identified almost perfectly.
In a 2015 study of 165 adults, how often people heard the illusion ranged from 0 to 100 percent, and it also varied with the video used.

title: Combining the senses
description: The brain integrates information from different senses, responding more strongly to sight and sound together; lip movements help most when the sound is poor.

facts.text: Information from different senses is integrated, and responses to combined stimuli, such as sight and sound, are typically stronger than the sum of each sense alone.
Watching a friend's lips helps you understand them at a loud concert; in a quiet cafe you would hardly need those visual cues.
The McGurk effect is reported to be strongest when the quality of the sound is poor.

title: Selective attention and shadowing
description: Selective attention picks some information to process and ignores the rest; in Colin Cherry's shadowing studies people knew little of the ignored message.

facts.text: Selective attention is the ability to select certain stimuli in the environment to process while ignoring distracting information.
Colin Cherry coined the term cocktail-party problem in a 1953 paper and studied it by having listeners shadow, or repeat aloud, speech in one ear while ignoring the other.
In shadowing tasks, people could report little of the ignored message's content and often didn't notice when it switched language, such as from English to German.

title: The cocktail party effect
description: About a third of people notice their own name in a message they are ignoring, which suggests ignored speech is turned down rather than blocked.

facts.text: Moray (1959) and a 1995 repeat by Wood and Cowan found that about 33 percent of people reported hearing their own name in a message they were ignoring.
Anne Treisman proposed that ignored information is weakened rather than completely blocked, so highly meaningful words such as your name can still get through.
In a preregistered 2021 replication, 29 percent of participants noticed their own name in the ignored message, while unexpected words were rarely detected.
People who noticed their name tended to score lower on working-memory tests, which researchers read as more trouble blocking out distracting information.

title: Inattentional blindness
description: Failing to notice something fully visible because attention is on something else, shown when about half of viewers missed a gorilla while counting basketball passes.

facts.text: In Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris's 1999 study, viewers counted basketball passes by a team in white while a person in a gorilla costume walked through the game.
Nearly half of the people who watched did not notice the gorilla at all, though it was clearly visible, because they were focused on counting passes and tuned out other visual information.
Inattentional blindness is the failure to notice something completely visible because a person is attending to something else.

Noticing depended on how similar the unexpected object was to the others and on how hard the counting task was, but not on how close it came to the attended action, suggesting people attend to objects and events rather than places.

title: Experts miss the unexpected too
description: In 2013, 83 percent of radiologists searching lung scans missed an inserted gorilla, and most of them had looked right at it.

facts.text: In a 2013 study, 83 percent of 24 radiologists searching lung scans for nodules missed a gorilla 48 times the size of an average nodule.
Eye tracking showed that most of the radiologists who missed the gorilla had looked directly at its location.

title: Task switching and switch costs
description: What feels like multitasking is often rapid switching, and each switch costs time and accuracy; preparation shrinks the cost but doesn't remove it.

facts.text: Some researchers suggest that, unless a task is fully automatic, multitasking is really rapid switching of attention back and forth between tasks.
Right after switching tasks, people respond substantially slower and usually make more errors; time to prepare shrinks this switch cost but doesn't eliminate it.
In a 2001 study by Rubinstein and colleagues, the time lost to switching grew as the rules of the tasks became more complex.

title: Phones, driving and divided attention
description: Phone conversations, handheld or hands-free, impair driving because they pull attention from the road; only about 1 in 40 people show no cost.

facts.text: In a 2001 driving-simulator study, handheld and hands-free phone conversations both doubled missed traffic signals and slowed reactions, while radio or a book on tape did not disrupt driving.
In later eye-tracking studies, drivers talking on a phone were less likely to later recognize objects they had looked at, a form of inattentional blindness.
In a 2010 simulator study of 200 people, 2.5 percent, about 1 in 40, showed no drop in performance when driving while doing a demanding memory and math task; the vast majority got worse.

title: Subliminal perception
description: A message below the threshold of awareness is subliminal. People can process some such information in the lab, but its effect on behavior is small and depends on existing goals.

facts.text: The absolute threshold is the minimum amount of stimulus energy that must be present for a stimulus to be detected 50 percent of the time.
A message below the threshold for conscious awareness is subliminal: it is received, but the person is not consciously aware of it.
In laboratory settings people can process and respond to information outside awareness, but hidden messages have little effect on behavior outside the lab.
In a 2006 study, subliminally flashing the drink brand Lipton Ice increased choice of that brand, but only among participants who were thirsty.

title: The subliminal popcorn hoax
description: In 1957 James Vicary claimed hidden "Eat Popcorn" messages in a cinema raised sales; he later admitted the study was made up, and no one has replicated it.

facts.text: In 1957 market researcher James Vicary claimed that briefly flashing the message "Eat Popcorn" during a movie, below conscious awareness, raised popcorn sales by more than 50 percent; it became one of the most famous claims for subliminal persuasion.
Vicary later admitted the study was made up; nobody has ever replicated his findings, and the study is regarded as a hoax.

title: Attention as a limited resource
description: Attention selects a little from a lot: William James wrote in 1890 that it implies withdrawal from some things to deal with others, and psychologists describe it as limited capacity.

facts.text: In 1890 William James wrote that attention "implies withdrawal from some things in order to deal effectively with others."
Psychologists describe attention as having limited capacity: people can attend to, or be aware of, only a small amount of information at a time.

title: Pavlov's accidental discovery
description: Studying digestion, the physiologist Ivan Pavlov noticed his dogs drooling before food arrived, a learned response he set out to test.

facts.text: Ivan Pavlov, a Russian physiologist, won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on the physiology of digestion.

While studying digestion, Pavlov measured how much saliva dogs produced in response to food, and noticed they began to salivate at the sight of food, at an empty food bowl and even at the sound of lab assistants' footsteps.
Salivating to food in the mouth is a reflex that involves no learning, but dogs don't naturally salivate at an empty bowl or at footsteps, so those responses were learned.

title: Classical conditioning
description: A neutral stimulus repeatedly paired just before an unconditioned stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus that triggers a learned, conditioned response on its own.

facts.text: In Pavlov's experiments, meat powder was an unconditioned stimulus, one that triggers a reflex, and the dogs' salivation to it was an unconditioned response, a natural, unlearned reaction.
Pavlov sounded a tone, a neutral stimulus that at first caused no salivation, just before giving the dogs meat powder; after he paired them over and over, the tone alone made the dogs salivate.
Once a neutral stimulus triggers the response on its own, it is called a conditioned stimulus, and the learned response to it is called a conditioned response.
Pavlov trained hungry dogs to salivate at sounds such as a metronome or a buzzer that had been associated with food.
Classical conditioning is a process by which organisms learn to associate stimuli and, as a result, to anticipate events.
Behaviorism, founded by John B. Watson, drew on Pavlov's classical conditioning, and Watson believed the same principles could be used to condition human emotions.

title: Extinction
description: When a conditioned stimulus keeps appearing without the unconditioned stimulus, the conditioned response weakens and disappears.

facts.text: When Pavlov sounded the tone without giving meat powder, the dogs soon stopped responding; this decrease in the conditioned response when the unconditioned stimulus no longer follows the conditioned stimulus is called extinction.
During extinction the conditioned response grows weaker and weaker until there is no response at all.

title: Spontaneous recovery: extinction is new learning
description: An extinguished response returns after a rest (spontaneous recovery) or in the original setting (renewal), because extinction adds new, context-dependent learning rather than erasing the old.

facts.text: After a couple of hours of rest from extinction training, Pavlov's dogs again salivated at the sound; Pavlov called this return of an extinguished conditioned response after a rest spontaneous recovery.
Extinction does not destroy the original learning; instead, it creates new learning that depends strongly on context.
An extinguished response tends to reappear after time passes, called spontaneous recovery, or when the animal is back in the context of the original learning, called renewal.

title: Little Albert and conditioned fear
description: In 1920 Watson and Rayner paired a loud noise with a white rat until an infant, Albert B., feared the rat.

facts.text: In 1920, John B. Watson and his graduate student Rosalie Rayner, at Johns Hopkins University, set out to condition fear in an infant their paper called Albert B., now known as Little Albert.
Before conditioning, Albert showed no fear of a white rat, a rabbit, a dog, masks or cotton wool.
A loud sound, made by striking a hammer on a steel bar behind Albert, frightened him and made him cry.
Watson struck the bar each time Albert touched the white rat; after the sound and the rat were paired repeatedly, the rat alone frightened him.

title: Stimulus generalization
description: A conditioned response spreads to stimuli that resemble the conditioned stimulus, as Albert's fear spread from the rat to other furry things.

facts.text: Days later, Albert was also afraid of other furry things, including a rabbit, a fur coat and a Santa Claus mask.
Stimulus generalization is giving the conditioned response to stimuli that are similar to the conditioned stimulus; the more similar a stimulus is, the more likely the response.

title: Why the Little Albert study is criticized
description: The study used one infant, never removed his fears, would be unethical today, and his identity is still disputed.

facts.text: Watson and Rayner's fear conditioning study was carried out on a single infant.
Watson and Rayner planned to remove Albert's conditioned fears, but he left the hospital on the last day of testing, so the fears were never removed.
The Little Albert study would be considered unethical by today's standards.
In 2009 one research team identified Little Albert as a particular boy, and in 2014 another team argued that a different boy matched the records better, so his identity is disputed.

title: Conditioned taste aversion
description: A food's taste linked with later illness becomes aversive, often after one pairing and across a delay of hours.

facts.text: In conditioned taste aversion, something eaten becomes linked with the nausea or illness that follows: the taste acts as the conditioned stimulus, and feeling sick at it is the conditioned response.
A taste aversion can be acquired after a single pairing of a taste with illness.
Most conditioning needs only a brief interval between the conditioned and unconditioned stimulus, but a taste aversion can form even when several hours pass between eating and getting sick.

title: Biology shapes what is easy to learn
description: Garcia and Koelling (1966) showed rats readily link tastes with illness and lights and sounds with pain, a biological constraint on conditioning.

facts.text: In a 1966 study, John Garcia and Robert Koelling gave thirsty rats flavored water accompanied by lights and sounds, followed by either illness or foot shocks; rats made ill avoided the flavor but not the lights and sounds, while shocked rats avoided the lights and sounds but not the flavor.
Taste aversion may be an evolutionary adaptation that helps animals quickly learn to avoid harmful foods, and Garcia and Koelling's results showed there are biological constraints on learning.

title: Thorndike's law of effect
description: Behaviors followed by satisfying consequences become more likely, and those followed by unpleasant ones less likely.

facts.text: Classical conditioning works on reflexive behaviors an organism already has, and it doesn't account for new behaviors such as riding a bike.
Edward Thorndike placed a cat in a box with a lever that, when pressed, opened a door so the cat could escape and get food.
Thorndike's law of effect states that behaviors followed by satisfying consequences are more likely to be repeated, and behaviors followed by unpleasant consequences are less likely to be repeated.

title: Operant conditioning
description: Learning to link a behavior with its consequence, studied by Skinner with rats and pigeons in the Skinner box.

facts.text: Building on the law of effect, B. F. Skinner experimented mainly on rats and pigeons in an operant conditioning chamber, the Skinner box, where a rat could press a lever or a pigeon peck a disk for food while a recorder counted the responses.
In operant conditioning, organisms learn to associate a behavior with its consequence, which comes soon after the behavior; in classical conditioning, the stimulus comes just before the response.

title: Shaping
description: Rewarding closer and closer approximations of a target behavior builds complex behaviors step by step.

facts.text: In shaping, successive approximations of a target behavior are rewarded: first any response resembling it, then only closer ones, until only the target behavior is reinforced; animal trainers commonly use it today.
Using shaping, Skinner taught pigeons to turn in circles, walk in figure eights and even play ping pong.

title: Reinforcement and punishment, positive and negative
description: Positive adds and negative removes; reinforcement increases a behavior and punishment decreases it, giving four combinations.

facts.text: In operant conditioning, positive means something is added and negative means something is taken away; they do not mean good and bad.
Reinforcement increases a behavior and punishment decreases a behavior.
In positive reinforcement, a desirable stimulus is added to increase a behavior, such as promising a child a toy for cleaning a room.
In negative reinforcement, an undesirable stimulus is removed to increase a behavior: a car's seatbelt alarm beeps until you fasten your seatbelt, making buckling up more likely.
In positive punishment, an undesirable stimulus is added to decrease a behavior, such as scolding a student to stop texting in class.
In negative punishment, a pleasant stimulus is removed to decrease a behavior, such as taking away a favorite toy; time-out, which removes a child from a desirable activity, works on this principle.
Negative reinforcement is often confused with punishment, but reinforcement, even when negative, always increases a behavior, while punishment always decreases it.

title: Reinforcement schedules
description: Rewards can come every time (continuous) or only sometimes (partial), on fixed or variable ratio or interval schedules.

facts.text: In continuous reinforcement a behavior is reinforced every time it occurs; in partial, or intermittent, reinforcement it is reinforced only some of the time.
Partial reinforcement schedules are fixed or variable, and ratio, based on the number of responses between reinforcements, or interval, based on the time between them.

Fixed ratio reinforces after a predictable number of responses, variable ratio after an unpredictable number, fixed interval at predictable time intervals, and variable interval at unpredictable time intervals.

title: Why unpredictable rewards last
description: Variable ratio schedules, used in most gambling, produce the most persistent behavior and are the hardest to extinguish.

facts.text: Most types of gambling reinforce on a variable ratio schedule, which is one reason gambling is so resistant to extinction.
Among the reinforcement schedules, variable ratio is the most productive and the most resistant to extinction, while fixed interval is the least productive and the easiest to extinguish.
Behaviors rewarded only intermittently persist longer once rewards stop than behaviors rewarded every time, an effect long seen as fundamental to why people keep gambling without winning.

title: Observational learning
description: Learning by watching a model and imitating, which Bandura described in four steps: attention, retention, reproduction and motivation.

facts.text: In observational learning, people and animals learn by watching others and then imitating, or modeling, what they do; the people performing the behavior are called models.
Albert Bandura argued that pure behaviorism could not explain why learning can happen without external reinforcement, and his social learning theory took mental processes into account.
Bandura described four steps in modeling: attention, retention, reproduction and motivation.
Seeing a model reinforced for a behavior makes an observer more motivated to copy it, which is called vicarious reinforcement.

title: The Bobo doll study
description: In 1961, preschoolers who watched an adult attack a Bobo doll later copied the attack's specific moves and words.

facts.text: In a 1961 study, Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross had 72 children from the Stanford University Nursery School, aged about three to five, watch an adult who either attacked a 5-foot inflated Bobo doll or played quietly.
The aggressive model struck the doll with a mallet, sat on it and punched it, and said things like 'Pow' and 'Sock him', distinctive acts children were unlikely to invent on their own.

Tested later in a different room with toys that included a Bobo doll, and with no model present, children who had watched the aggressive model reproduced much aggression resembling the model's, far more than children who saw the quiet model or no model.

title: Learning versus performance
description: Seeing a model punished reduced copying, but rewards revealed the children had learned the behavior anyway: consequences shape doing more than learning.

facts.text: In a 1965 study, children who saw a model punished for attacking the Bobo doll imitated the aggression less than children who saw the model rewarded or facing no consequence.

When Bandura then offered the children rewards for reproducing the model's behavior, the differences between the groups disappeared, showing that the children had learned the behavior even when they had not performed it.

title: How habits form
description: Repeating a response in the same context, with a reward, strengthens a link between context cues and the response until the cue triggers it automatically.

facts.text: Habits form as people pursue goals by repeating the same response in a given context.
With each repetition, the link in memory between context cues, such as a coffee filter, and the response gradually strengthens, until the cues automatically activate the habit.
The reward that follows a response strengthens the link between context cues and the response; habit learning builds on Thorndike's principle that rewarded responses are repeated.

title: How long a habit takes
description: In Lally's 2010 study, new daily behaviors took a median of 66 days to become automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days.

facts.text: In a 2010 study led by Phillippa Lally, 96 volunteers chose an eating, drinking or activity behavior to carry out daily in the same context, such as after breakfast, for 12 weeks.
In Lally's study, the time for a behavior to reach near its maximum automaticity had a median of 66 days and ranged from 18 to an estimated 254 days.
In Lally's study, missing one opportunity to perform the behavior did not materially affect habit formation.

title: What learning is, and its three basic forms
description: Learning is a relatively permanent change from experience; classical conditioning, operant conditioning and observational learning are its three basic forms.

facts.text: Learning is a relatively permanent change in behavior or knowledge that results from experience.

Associative learning happens when an organism makes connections between stimuli or events that occur together, and it is central to classical conditioning, operant conditioning and observational learning.
In classical and operant conditioning, learning happens only through direct experience, while observational learning happens by watching others and imitating them.

title: Three stages of memory
description: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model (1968) routes information through sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory, with sensory memory lasting only a couple of seconds.

facts.text: In 1968, Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin proposed that information passes through three stages to be stored (sensory, short-term and long-term memory), a model that treats memory like a computer processing information; it is not the only memory model.

Sensory memory stores brief sensory events such as sights, sounds and tastes for up to a couple of seconds; we cannot absorb most of it, discard what we do not view as valuable, and pass on what we do to short-term memory.

title: Rehearsal into long-term memory
description: Short-term memory lasts about 15 to 30 seconds; rehearsal, by repetition or by linking to what you know, moves information into long-term memory, whose capacity is believed unlimited.

facts.text: Short-term memory holds information for about 15 to 30 seconds, after which it either goes to long-term memory or is discarded.

Rehearsal moves information from short-term to long-term memory: active rehearsal repeats it, and elaborative rehearsal links it to what you already know, such as a new phone number sharing a relative's area code.
Long-term memory is the continuous storage of information, and its capacity is believed to be unlimited.

title: Working memory and its limit
description: Working memory holds the few thoughts in use right now; Miller's 1956 "seven, plus or minus two" is now usually revised to about four chunks.

facts.text: Short-term memory is best seen as one component of working memory, the few thoughts held active at a time and used in tasks such as understanding a sentence, carrying a digit in mental arithmetic and planning the order of errands.
In 1956, George Miller reviewed the research on short-term memory, found people can hold between 5 and 9 items, and called the capacity "the magical number seven, plus or minus two".
When rehearsal and grouping are prevented, young adults hold only about 3 to 5 chunks in working memory, and contemporary research, led by Nelson Cowan and others, puts its capacity at about 4.

title: Chunking
description: Grouping items into meaningful units lets each slot of working memory hold more, as when ten digits become three chunks.

facts.text: Chunking organizes information into manageable units: instead of remembering 5205550467 you remember 520-555-0467.

In Cowan's studies, arbitrary word pairs learned together, such as desk-ball, became new chunks: young adults recalled about the same number of chunks whether these were learned pairs or single words.
To remember to buy bread, milk and pepper, you can form a single chunk by imagining bread floating in peppery milk.

title: Explicit and implicit memory
description: Explicit memories (episodic and semantic) are consciously recalled and can be put into words; implicit memories such as skills show up in performance.

facts.text: Explicit (declarative) memories are those we consciously recall and can put into words; they include episodic memory for events we lived, like a last birthday, and semantic memory for facts and word meanings.
Implicit memories are not consciously recalled but show up in performance; procedural memory, for skills like riding a bicycle or brushing your teeth, is a kind you usually cannot put into words.

title: The case of H.M.
description: Henry Molaison (H.M.) lost the ability to form new explicit memories after 1953 surgery yet still learned skills, showing that memory has separate systems.

facts.text: In 1953, at age 27, H.M. had surgery on both sides of his brain to control severe seizures; afterward he forgot daily events almost as fast as they happened, though he kept most older memories from before the operation.
Despite his profound amnesia, H.M.'s IQ was above average and his immediate memory, like holding a phone number briefly, was intact.
To protect his privacy, H.M. was known only by his initials; his full name, Henry Gustav Molaison, was disclosed only after his death in 2008.
Brenda Milner tested H.M. on mirror drawing: he improved over repeated trials across 3 days and kept the skill, yet had no recollection of having done the task before.
H.M. is probably the best known single patient in the history of neuroscience, and his memory was studied for five decades until his death in 2008.

H.M.'s case showed that memory is divided into systems: the region removed in his surgery is critical for forming long-term memories of facts and events, while motor skill learning relies on other brain networks.
Asked how he felt about all the tests, H.M. replied, "What they find out about me helps them to help other people."

title: Context-dependent memory
description: A retrieval cue works best when it matches how a memory was encoded, and the setting of learning can act as a cue; the effect on recall is real but often weak.

facts.text: The encoding specificity principle (Tulving and Thomson, 1973) says a retrieval cue works to the extent that it matches the way a memory was encoded, as when an old song brings back the party where you heard it.
In 1975, Godden and Baddeley had divers learn lists of spoken words on land or underwater and recall them in the same place or the other; recall was much better when the two places matched.
The effect of environmental context on free recall is well established, but in many situations it is rather weak.

title: The divers study and its retest
description: Godden and Baddeley's 1975 land-and-underwater study became a textbook classic, but a 2021 replication found no same-place advantage.

facts.text: Virtually all cognitive psychology and memory textbooks describe Godden and Baddeley's divers study as the classic example of context-dependent memory.
In a 2021 replication, Jaap Murre had 16 divers learn words on land or in a heated indoor pool and found no advantage for recalling them in the same place.
The original divers study used cold open water off Scotland rather than a shallow heated pool, and Murre concluded that more replications are needed to settle whether the classic result holds.

title: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve
description: Testing himself with nonsense syllables, Ebbinghaus (1885) found forgetting is steep soon after learning and then levels out; a 2015 replication matched his curve.

facts.text: Hermann Ebbinghaus used only himself as a subject; his forgetting curve rests on about seven months of experimenting, often up to three sessions a day.
In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus published his book on memory, reporting experiments on himself with nonsense syllables that produced the forgetting curve.

Ebbinghaus first tried learning stanzas of Byron's Don Juan but found their meanings too variable for fair measurement, so he introduced nonsense syllables such as dax, bap and rif, which were more uniform.
Ebbinghaus's famous forgetting curve shows memory for new information decaying quickly at first and then leveling out, so most forgetting happens soon after learning.

In 2015, Jaap Murre and a colleague at the University of Amsterdam replicated the experiment, with one subject spending 70 hours learning and relearning lists; the results were similar to Ebbinghaus's.

title: The savings method
description: Ebbinghaus measured memory by how much less time it took to relearn a list, which can reveal traces that recall tests miss.

facts.text: Ebbinghaus learned each row of syllables until he could recite it twice without error, then relearned it after 20 minutes to 31 days; the time saved on relearning (for example 25 repetitions down to 20, a 20% saving) measured what memory remained.
The savings method can show that something was retained even when an ordinary recall test would show nothing, because relearning goes faster.

title: The testing effect
description: Retrieving a memory strengthens it: practice tests beat restudying on delayed tests, even though restudying feels more reassuring.

facts.text: In a 2006 study by Roediger and Karpicke, students read prose passages, then took recall tests or restudied; restudying did better after 5 minutes, but tested students remembered substantially more after 2 days or a week, though restudying made students more confident.
The act of retrieving a memory makes it much more likely to be retrieved again, a phenomenon called the testing effect or retrieval practice effect.
Most students report rereading and highlighting, but the 2013 review rated both low utility because they do not consistently boost performance, and advised practice testing instead of rereading.

title: The spacing effect
description: Spreading study over several sessions beats cramming; with practice testing, it earned the top rating in a 2013 review of study techniques.

facts.text: Distributed practice means studying across time in short sessions rather than cramming; memory consolidation takes time, and spacing study out allows memories to consolidate.
The spacing effect, better long-term memory when learning is spaced out rather than massed, was first studied by Ebbinghaus and is arguably the most replicable finding in experimental psychology.

A 2013 review led by John Dunlosky rated ten study techniques; only practice testing and distributed practice earned a high utility rating, because they helped learners of different ages and abilities across many kinds of tasks.

title: Memory as reconstruction
description: Bartlett's War of the Ghosts studies (1932), replicated in 1999, showed that recalling rebuilds an event rather than replaying it, so errors creep in.

facts.text: In his 1932 book Remembering, Frederic Bartlett reported having participants, probably English college students, hear the Native American folktale "The War of the Ghosts" and recall it after 15 minutes and again weeks, months or even years later.
The War of the Ghosts is disjointed, contains supernatural elements and is rather difficult to understand.
Bartlett argued that comprehending an event is a construction, so recalling it later requires reconstructing it rather than replaying a copy.

Earlier attempts to repeat Bartlett's study had failed, but in 1999 Erik Bergman and Henry Roediger replicated it; six months after hearing the story, most of what people recalled was distorted in some way.

title: Schemas in memory
description: Schemas, organized knowledge about how things usually go, guide remembering and reshape unfamiliar details toward the familiar.

facts.text: In Bartlett's studies the retold stories got shorter and changed systematically: people rationalized the bizarre elements, sometimes adding details to explain them, reshaping the story toward their own schemas, and these errors grew over retellings.
A typical change in retellings of The War of the Ghosts replaced unfamiliar details with familiar ones, such as "canoe" becoming "boat".

Bartlett argued that remembering is guided by schemas, general organizing structures that aid encoding and guide retrieval but can also cause errors, such as recalling a beach umbrella in a beach scene that had none.

title: The misinformation effect
description: Misleading information after an event, even one word in a question, can alter memory of the event (Loftus and Palmer, 1974).

facts.text: In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer asked students who saw car crash films how fast the cars went when they "smashed", "hit", "contacted" (or similar) each other; "smashed" drew higher estimates and, a week later, over twice as many reports of broken glass never shown.

In the misinformation effect, misleading information met after an event contaminates memory of the event; hundreds of studies have shown it, for details as small as a feature of a face and objects as large as a barn that was not there.
In a 1975 study by Loftus, people were more likely to say yes when asked "Did you see the broken headlight?" than "Did you see a broken headlight?"

title: Implanted false memories
description: Suggestion can create memories of whole events that never happened, as in the lost-in-the-mall study (1995), which a 2023 replication supported.

facts.text: In a 1995 study by Loftus and Pickrell, students were asked about four childhood events supposedly supplied by relatives; one, getting lost in a shopping mall, was invented, and after repeated questioning a quarter of them came to believe it had happened.
A preregistered 2023 replication with 123 participants coded 35% of them as reporting a false memory of getting lost in a mall, compared with 25% in the original study.
Once false memories are implanted, whether by complex or simple methods, they are extremely difficult to tell apart from true memories.

title: Eyewitness confidence
description: A witness's certainty can grow after the event, especially after confirming feedback, so confidence at trial can be high even when an identification is wrong.

facts.text: In 1984 in North Carolina, a witness identified Ronald Cotton from photos and a lineup, and her testimony helped convict him; after more than 10 years in prison he was exonerated by DNA evidence.

At the photo lineup the witness first said "I think this is the guy," the detective told her she did great, and by the trial she had absolutely no doubt; Gary Wells points to suggestive procedures such as confirming a witness's choice.

In a 1998 study by Gary Wells and Amy Bradfield, people watched a store security video and picked someone from a lineup that did not contain the culprit; those told "Good, you identified the suspect" later reported being more certain.
A 2014 meta-analysis covering about 7,000 participants found that confirming feedback reliably inflates what witnesses later report about their certainty, their view of the event and their attention.

title: Fairer lineups
description: Double-blind, fair lineups with confidence recorded at once make eyewitness identifications more trustworthy.

facts.text: In a double-blind lineup, the person running it does not know which member is the suspect, so they cannot give the witness leading cues.
In a fair lineup, every member matches the eyewitness's description, so no one sticks out and the suspect is no more likely to be picked by someone who did not see the crime.
Researchers recommend recording a witness's confidence and other judgments right away, before any feedback can occur.

Under clean conditions (a fair lineup, no administrator influence and an immediate confidence statement on a first test), high-confidence identifications are remarkably accurate, while initial low-confidence ones are error prone.

title: Encoding, storage and retrieval
description: Memory has three jobs (getting information in, keeping it and getting it back), and memory failures can be traced to each, as the penny study shows for encoding.

facts.text: Memory is the set of processes used to encode, store and retrieve information: encoding puts information in, storage keeps it, and retrieval gets it back into awareness.

In a 1979 study by Raymond Nickerson and Marilyn Adams, most Americans could not pick out an accurate US penny from similar drawings, because they had encoded only enough detail to tell it from other coins.
Distraction during learning impairs later memory, because information that is never encoded cannot be remembered.
Memory, even for vivid events, is not like a video recording: its parts are stored in different places and put back together when you remember, and each step is a chance for error.

title: Drives and homeostasis
description: Motivation is what directs behavior toward a goal; drive theory says a slip from the body's balance (homeostasis) creates a need felt as a drive, such as hunger, that pushes behavior until balance returns, and what worked becomes a habit.

facts.text: Motivation describes the wants or needs that direct behavior toward a goal.
Homeostasis is the tendency to maintain a balance, or optimal level, within a biological system.
In drive theory, a deviation from homeostasis creates a need and a drive that directs behavior: low blood sugar produces hunger, and eating restores balance.
Drive theory holds that once a behavior has successfully reduced a drive, we are more likely to use that behavior again when the drive returns.

title: Incentives pull, drives push
description: Incentive theory says rewards and goals out in the world pull behavior toward them, while drives push from within; the two jointly shape behavior, and incentives can work even without a drive.

facts.text: Incentive theory says rewards and other outside goals pull behavior toward them, while drives from internal needs push it; the two jointly determine behavior.
An animal in a Skinner box normally presses a bar for water when deprived of water, but under special conditions it will press the bar to drink even when not deprived.

title: Maslow's hierarchy of needs
description: In 1943 Abraham Maslow proposed a hierarchy of needs from physiological needs through safety, love and belonging, and esteem up to self-actualization, with lower needs coming first.

facts.text: In a 1943 paper in Psychological Review, Abraham Maslow proposed a hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualization.
In Maslow's theory, lower-level needs generally take priority over higher ones: someone struggling to find enough food is unlikely to focus on how others see them.
Maslow described self-actualization as the desire to become more and more what one is, to become everything that one is capable of becoming.

title: What later research changed about Maslow
description: Maslow never drew a pyramid (Charles McDermid did, in 1960), he said the order is not rigid, and a 2011 study across 123 countries found each need linked to wellbeing largely regardless of the others.

facts.text: In the same 1943 paper, Maslow wrote that his hierarchy is "not nearly as rigid" as he may have implied, and that most people have each of their needs only partly satisfied.
Maslow never presented his hierarchy as a pyramid; a 2019 history by Todd Bridgman and colleagues traced the pyramid to consulting psychologist Charles McDermid's 1960 article.
A 2011 study by Louis Tay and Ed Diener across 123 countries found that meeting each need was linked to wellbeing largely regardless of whether other needs were met.

title: Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation
description: Intrinsic motivation is doing something for the satisfaction it brings; extrinsic motivation is doing it to get something from others.

facts.text: Intrinsically motivated behavior is performed for the personal satisfaction it brings; extrinsically motivated behavior is performed to receive something from others.

title: The overjustification effect
description: An expected, tangible reward for something people already enjoy can reduce their later interest, as Lepper's 1973 marker study and a 1999 meta-analysis of 128 studies showed; praise and surprise rewards tend not to.

facts.text: In a 1973 study at Stanford's Bing Nursery School, Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett offered preschoolers who already liked drawing with magic markers a Good Player Award.
One to two weeks later, children who had drawn for an expected award spent about 8.6 percent of free time drawing, about half as much as children given a surprise award or none.
The overjustification effect is the loss of intrinsic motivation when extrinsic motivation is given, which can make continued effort depend on the reward.
A 1999 meta-analysis of 128 studies by Edward Deci, Richard Koestner and Richard Ryan found that expected and tangible rewards undermined intrinsic motivation, while positive feedback enhanced it.
Tangible rewards such as money tend to harm intrinsic motivation more than praise, and when a reward comes as a surprise rather than an expectation, intrinsic motivation tends to persist.

title: The ego depletion theory
description: Ego depletion is the idea that self-control draws on a limited resource that exertion uses up; its classic 1998 test had hungry people eat radishes instead of cookies and then give up sooner on puzzles.

facts.text: In a 1998 study by Roy Baumeister and colleagues, hungry people ate radishes while resisting chocolates and chocolate chip cookies baked in the room; a few sniffed the cookies, but none bit.
Afterward, radish eaters persisted about 8 minutes on unsolvable puzzles, compared with about 19 minutes for chocolate eaters and about 21 for a group given no food.
Baumeister's team concluded that self-control draws on a limited inner resource that exertion uses up, a state called ego depletion.

title: Why ego depletion failed replication
description: Multi-lab tests of ego depletion in 2016 (23 labs) and 2021 (36 labs) found an effect near zero, so the idea is no longer treated as settled.

facts.text: An early meta-analysis of ego-depletion experiments found a medium-sized effect, but later meta-analyses questioned its size and existence and found signs of possible bias.
In 2016, a replication led by Martin Hagger ran one standardized ego-depletion test in 23 labs with 2,141 participants and found an effect near zero.
A 2021 test led by Kathleen Vohs in 36 labs with 3,531 participants did not find evidence for ego depletion in its planned analyses.

title: James-Lange and Cannon-Bard
description: The James-Lange theory says the feeling of emotion follows bodily arousal; the Cannon-Bard theory says arousal and feeling happen at the same time, independently.

facts.text: The James-Lange theory holds that emotions arise from physiological arousal: meeting a venomous snake makes your heart race, and only then do you feel fear.
The James-Lange theory also held that different patterns of arousal produce different feelings.
Doubting that arousal differs enough between emotions to explain them all, the Cannon-Bard theory proposed that arousal and the feeling of emotion occur at the same time but independently.

title: The two-factor theory of emotion
description: Schachter and Singer proposed that an emotion is bodily arousal plus a label drawn from the situation; their 1962 epinephrine experiment showed unexplained arousal taking on the mood of the people around.

facts.text: The Schachter-Singer two-factor theory says an emotion combines physiological arousal with a cognitive label: the arousal is interpreted in context to produce the emotion felt.

In 1962, Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer injected men with epinephrine, which mimics fight-or-flight; only some were told what to expect, and each waited with an actor who behaved euphorically or angrily.
Men told to expect the arousal reported no emotional change, while those not expecting it were more likely to report euphoria or anger matching the actor's behavior.

title: Ekman's universal expressions
description: Paul Ekman's studies, including a 1971 study with the Fore of Papua New Guinea who matched faces to stories, suggested a small set of facial expressions is recognized everywhere.

facts.text: In a 1971 study, Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen told members of the Fore people of Papua New Guinea short emotional stories and asked them to choose the photographed face that matched each one.
Matching tasks like this, run in small-scale societies with little outside contact, gave strong evidence that people in different cultures recognize the same expressions.

Supporters of universal expressions note that congenitally blind people move their faces in emotion much as sighted people do, and Ekman's side lists seven universal expressions: happiness, surprise, sadness, fear, disgust, contempt and anger.

title: The debate over universal expressions
description: Lisa Feldman Barrett and colleagues argue expressions vary widely by culture and situation and that choose-from-a-list methods inflated agreement; Jessica Tracy's team and others still find evidence for universality.

facts.text: A 2019 review led by Lisa Feldman Barrett found that people do smile when happy or scowl when angry more often than chance, but how people express emotions varies substantially across cultures, situations and people.

The review noted that most studies had people choose answers from a short list, which makes contrary evidence hard to find, and that where people in small-scale societies named faces freely, they rarely gave the expected emotion words.
Trobriand Islanders in Papua New Guinea read the wide-eyed, gasping face that Western studies call fear as a sign of threat or aggression.
Barrett proposed that emotions are constructed from experience, so the same bodily state can become different emotions depending on the situation.

In 2021, Jessica Tracy's team reported that the Mayangna of Nicaragua, an isolated small-scale society, recognized bodily expressions of anger, sadness and fear more often than chance, evidence they took for universality.
Researchers on both sides agree that facial movements carry a range of information and matter for social communication.

title: The facial feedback hypothesis
description: The facial feedback hypothesis says your expression can affect what you feel; its famous 1988 test had people hold a pen in their mouth in a smile-like or blocking position while rating cartoons.

facts.text: The facial feedback hypothesis proposes that your facial expression can affect the emotion you experience.

In 1988, Fritz Strack and colleagues had people hold a pen in their mouth in ways that engaged or blocked the smiling muscles, without asking them to smile; the smile position made cartoons seem funnier.

title: Facial feedback's mixed replication record
description: A 17-lab replication of the pen study found almost no effect in 2016, while a 2019 meta-analysis and the 2022 Many Smiles study found small effects of deliberately posed smiles.

facts.text: In 2016, 17 labs led by Eric-Jan Wagenmakers repeated the pen study with one shared protocol; the original's 0.82-point funniness difference on a 10-point scale shrank to 0.03.
A 2019 meta-analysis led by Nicholas Coles concluded that facial feedback has a small but highly variable effect on emotional experience.

In 2022 the Many Smiles Collaboration, including researchers who disagreed, tested 3,878 people in 19 countries: copying smiling faces or deliberately posing a smile raised happiness, while the pen method was less conclusive.

title: Sleep loss, attention and judgment
description: Losing sleep impairs attention, decisions and memory, more so the more sleep is lost; 17 to 19 hours awake can match 0.05 percent blood alcohol, and people on short sleep underrate their own impairment.

facts.text: Sleep deprivation impairs the ability to maintain attention, make decisions and recall long-term memories, and the impairments grow more severe as sleep loss increases.
In a 2000 study, after 17 to 19 hours without sleep, performance on some tests was equal to or worse than at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.05 percent.
In a 2003 lab study by Hans Van Dongen and colleagues, adults allowed 6 hours or less in bed a night for 14 days built up thinking deficits equal to up to 2 nights of total sleep deprivation.
Their ratings of their own sleepiness rose only a little after the first days, suggesting they were largely unaware of their growing deficits.

title: Sleep loss and emotion
description: Without sleep, the brain overreacts to negative events and struggles to keep emotions in context: in a 2007 study, 35 hours awake made emotional centers over 60 percent more reactive.

facts.text: In a 2007 brain-imaging study by Matthew Walker's team, people kept awake about 35 hours had emotional brain centers over 60 percent more reactive to disturbing images than rested people.
Walker's team concluded that without sleep the brain was less able to put emotional experiences into context and produce controlled, appropriate responses.

title: Freud's dream interpretation
description: Freud saw dreams as a route to the unconscious and split them into manifest content (the storyline) and latent content (the hidden meaning).

facts.text: Freud believed dreams gave access to the unconscious, and he distinguished a dream's manifest content, its storyline, from its latent content, the hidden meaning he thought lay beneath.

title: What dream content research shows
description: Counting what happens in large sets of dream reports shows most dreams are realistic, often negative in tone, and continuous with the dreamer's general waking concerns rather than coded messages.

facts.text: Calvin Hall and Robert Van de Castle built a system for counting what happens in dreams and set norms in 1966 from five dreams each of 100 men and 100 women students in Cleveland, Ohio.
A study of 635 dream reports collected in a sleep lab described the typical dream as a clear, coherent story of a realistic situation, with the dreamer and other people doing very ordinary things.

In the Hall and Van de Castle norms, 80 percent of men's and 77 percent of women's dreams have at least one negative element, such as aggression, misfortune or a negative emotion; 53 percent have a positive one.
Dream content tends to follow the dreamer's general waking concerns and main relationships, though not the specific events of the day.
In a study by Rosalind Cartwright, women going through divorce who thought more about their former spouse while awake dreamed about that person more often.

title: The parts of an emotion
description: An emotion combines a subjective experience, an expression, an appraisal of the situation and a bodily response; how you appraise an event shapes the feeling, so two people can feel differently about the same moment.

facts.text: Psychologists describe an emotion as a combination of subjective experience, expression, cognitive appraisal and physiological responses.
Appraisal theory holds that your thoughts about an event come before the emotion and shape it, so two people can feel differently about the same event.
An emotion is relatively intense and occurs in response to something, while a mood is longer-lasting, less intense and not a response to a particular event.

title: System 1 and System 2
description: Psychologists describe two modes of thinking: fast, automatic, effortless System 1 and slower, effortful, deliberate System 2, which can override intuitive judgments.

facts.text: Stanovich and West (2000) labeled two types of thinking System 1 and System 2: System 1 is fast, automatic, effortless and hard to control, with features similar to perception; System 2 is slower, effortful and deliberately controlled.
Kahneman described most judgments as normally intuitive, produced by System 1, but they can be modified or overridden by the deliberate operations of System 2.
Daniel Kahneman, a psychologist who worked with Amos Tversky, shared the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics and gave his Nobel lecture, "Maps of Bounded Rationality", in December 2002.

title: The unchecked intuitive answer
description: Puzzles like the bat and ball show that System 2 checks intuitive answers only laxly, so bright people often report a quick wrong answer; the Cognitive Reflection Test measures resisting that first answer.

facts.text: In the bat-and-ball puzzle (together $1.10, the bat costs $1 more than the ball), almost everyone first wants to say 10 cents, because $1.10 splits naturally into $1 and 10 cents; the ball actually costs 5 cents.
Shane Frederick found that 50 percent (47 of 93) of Princeton students and 56 percent (164 of 293) of University of Michigan students gave the wrong answer to the bat-and-ball puzzle.

One job of System 2 is to monitor the quality of mental operations, but Kahneman and Frederick suggested this monitoring is normally quite lax and lets many intuitive judgments through, including wrong ones.

In 2005 Frederick published the three-item Cognitive Reflection Test, which measures the ability or disposition to reflect on a question and resist the first response that comes to mind; errors on such puzzles predicted relative indifference to delayed rewards.

title: What a heuristic is
description: A heuristic is a mental shortcut or rule of thumb that saves time and energy but is not always the best method; Kahneman explained many heuristics as quietly swapping a hard question for an easier one.

facts.text: A heuristic is a mental shortcut, such as a rule of thumb, that saves time and energy when making a decision but is not always the best method for making a rational decision.
In a 1974 Science article, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described three heuristics of judgment: representativeness, availability and anchoring.

Kahneman explained judgment heuristics as attribute substitution: people evaluate a difficult attribute by substituting an easier, more accessible one, an automatic and effortless operation of System 1.

title: The availability heuristic
description: People judge how frequent or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid, memorable and widely reported events seem more common than they are.

facts.text: The availability heuristic judges the frequency or probability of an event by the ease with which instances come to mind.

Because words are easier to search by their first letter, most people judge words starting with a consonant such as r or k to be more common than words with it in third position, although r and k are more frequent in third position.
When people heard a list of famous men and women, they wrongly judged that the sex with the more famous names was more numerous on the list.
In Lichtenstein and colleagues' 1978 study of judged causes of death, college students judged tornadoes to be more frequent killers than asthma, although asthma was about 20 times more likely.

The 1978 study found the most overestimated causes of death were dramatic ones such as botulism, tornadoes, floods and homicide, while undramatic "quiet killers" such as asthma, diabetes and stroke were underestimated.
The researchers traced the errors to exposure, memorability and imaginability, including how often causes appeared in the news, and people could not correct the biases when told to avoid them.

title: Anchoring
description: An initial number, even an arbitrary one, pulls later estimates toward it because people adjust away from a starting point too little.

facts.text: Tversky and Kahneman demonstrated anchoring with a wheel of fortune marked from 0 to 100 but rigged to stop at 10 or 65; students then said whether the share of African nations in the UN was higher or lower than their number and gave a best guess.
The median estimates of the percentage of African countries in the UN were 25 for the group given 10 and 45 for the group given 65, and payoffs for accuracy did not reduce the anchoring effect.
In anchoring, people start from an initial value and adjust to reach an answer, but the adjustments are typically insufficient.

High school students given 5 seconds to estimate 8x7x6x5x4x3x2x1 gave a median of 2,250, while those shown 1x2x3x4x5x6x7x8 gave 512; the correct answer is 40,320. The first steps of the multiplication give a higher number in the descending order.

title: Anchoring survives replication
