description: Anchoring is one of the sturdiest findings on mental shortcuts: the 2014 Many Labs project replicated it across dozens of samples, while two priming effects failed.

facts.text: The Many Labs project (2014) retested 13 classic and newer effects across 36 samples totaling 6,344 participants; 10 replicated consistently, and two, flag priming and currency priming, did not replicate.
Anchoring was among the effects that replicated in the Many Labs project, which tested it with questions such as the height of Mount Everest and the population of Chicago.

title: The representativeness heuristic
description: People judge how likely something is by how much it resembles a typical case or stereotype, so a vivid description can beat the odds in our judgment.

facts.text: The representativeness heuristic judges something by how similar it seems to existing stereotypes or prior beliefs.

When people ranked Linda's possible jobs by resemblance and others ranked them by probability, the two rankings agreed almost perfectly; Linda resembles a feminist bank teller more than a stereotypical bank teller.

title: The Linda problem
description: In Tversky and Kahneman's Linda problem most people rated "bank teller and feminist" as more likely than "bank teller", and a later adversarial collaboration tested when the effect appears.

facts.text: The Linda problem describes Linda as 31, single, outspoken and very bright, a philosophy major who as a student was concerned with discrimination and social justice and took part in antinuclear demonstrations.

In Tversky and Kahneman's 1983 study, 85 percent of 142 University of British Columbia undergraduates judged "Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement" more probable than "Linda is a bank teller".
A conjunction such as "bank teller and feminist" cannot be more probable than one of its parts, "bank teller".

In 2001 Hertwig, who argued that frequency formats remove the Linda effect and that people read "and" differently, ran an adversarial collaboration with Kahneman: they agreed on tests in advance, with Barbara Mellers as arbiter.

Frequency formats alone did not eliminate the conjunction effect, but it disappeared with Hertwig's wording once filler items were removed; Kahneman and Hertwig still interpret the result differently.

title: The halo effect
description: One overall impression of a person colors judgments of their separate traits; Edward Thorndike named the effect in 1920 after studying army ratings.

facts.text: In 1920 Edward Thorndike reported that army ratings meant to judge physique, intelligence, leadership and character independently were too closely linked, as in one flight commander's ratings of 137 aviation cadets.
Thorndike called this constant error, in which a general impression of a person colors ratings of specific qualities, the "halo".

title: The halo works unnoticed
description: Nisbett and Wilson showed that liking a person changes how people rate even concrete traits like appearance and accent, and that they don't realize it.

facts.text: In 1977 Nisbett and Wilson showed students one of two taped interviews with the same French-speaking Belgian instructor, warm or cold; viewers of the warm version rated his appearance, mannerisms and accent appealing, and viewers of the cold version found them irritating.

The students were unaware that their overall liking changed their ratings; those who saw the cold instructor believed the influence ran the other way, that disliking his traits had lowered their overall opinion.

title: Wason's 2-4-6 task
description: In Peter Wason's 1960 rule-discovery task, most people tested only number sets that fit their own guess, so few found the true, broader rule without a wrong announcement first.

facts.text: In 1960 Peter Wason tested whether intelligent young adults seek only confirming evidence or also evidence that could eliminate their idea; only 6 of 29 found the correct rule without first announcing a wrong one.

In the 2, 4, 6 task, people propose sets of three numbers and hear whether each fits; they usually guess rules like "increasing by 2" and test sets such as 6, 8, 10, but the correct rule is simply increasing numbers.

title: The positive test strategy
description: Testing only cases you expect to fit your guess can never reveal a guess that is too narrow; Klayman and Ha argued this positive test strategy is often a good heuristic but fails in tasks like Wason's.

facts.text: Klayman and Ha (1987) showed that if your guess is "increasing by 2", every set that fits it also fits "increasing", so testing only fitting sets can never show the guess is wrong; a set expected to fail, like 2, 4, 7, is needed.
Wason interpreted his results as a preference for confirming evidence over evidence that could eliminate a hypothesis.

Klayman and Ha (1987) called this a positive test strategy and showed it can be a very good heuristic under realistic conditions, although it can lead to systematic errors when the true rule is broader than the guess.

title: Hindsight bias
description: After learning an outcome, people feel it was more predictable than it was and even misremember their own earlier predictions, as Fischhoff and Beyth showed with Nixon's trips.

facts.text: Hindsight bias is the feeling of having "known it all along": believing an event was more predictable after it became known than it was before.

Fischhoff and Beyth (1975) had people judge the probability of outcomes of President Nixon's forthcoming trips to Peking (Beijing) and Moscow; afterward, people remembered giving higher probabilities to events that happened and lower ones to events that did not.
Fischhoff and Beyth's 1975 paper was titled "I knew it would happen": Remembered probabilities of once-future things.

title: Why hindsight fools us
description: Hindsight bias comes from recalling what fits the outcome, mistaking ease of understanding for likelihood, and wanting an orderly world; it resists warnings, fuels overconfidence, and shrinks when people consider alternative explanations.

facts.text: Roese and Vohs trace hindsight bias to selectively recalling information that fits the outcome and making sense of it, to mistaking the ease of understanding an outcome for its prior likelihood, and to a need to see the world as orderly and predictable.
Fischhoff (1975) found that hindsight bias remained even when people were explicitly told to ignore what they knew about the outcome.
Hindsight bias has been featured in more than 800 scholarly papers, appears in people around the world, young and old, and has been documented in areas from medical diagnoses to terrorist attacks.
Consequences of hindsight bias include general overconfidence in the certainty of one's judgments, and encouraging people to consider alternative explanations for an outcome can reduce it.

title: Overconfidence about our own skills
description: Many people rate their own abilities more favorably than they can all be, as Svenson's drivers did.

facts.text: In Ola Svenson's 1981 study, 93 percent of a US sample and 69 percent of a Swedish sample believed they were more skillful drivers than the median driver in their group.
People tend to hold overly favorable views of their abilities in many social and intellectual domains.

title: The Dunning-Kruger debate
description: Kruger and Dunning reported that the least skilled overestimate themselves most, but critics argue the usual chart is partly a statistical artifact and the effect may be much smaller.

facts.text: In 1999 Kruger and Dunning found that people scoring in the bottom quarter on tests of humor, grammar and logic scored around the 12th percentile but estimated themselves at the 62nd, and argued their lack of skill also robbed them of the ability to notice it.
Critics argue the usual Dunning-Kruger chart, which averages self-ratings for four ability groups, is confounded by the better-than-average effect and regression toward the mean.

In 2020 Gignac and Zajenkowski tested 929 people on intelligence with other statistical methods, found no support for the Dunning-Kruger pattern, and concluded the effect may be much smaller than reported.

title: The slow-walking priming study
description: Bargh's 1996 finding that old-age words made people walk more slowly failed a careful 2012 replication, which traced the effect to experimenters' expectations.

facts.text: In a 1996 study by Bargh, Chen and Burrows, students unscrambled sentences containing words related to old age and then walked more slowly down the hallway when leaving, reportedly without noticing the link.
The slow-walking study was instrumental in spreading the view in social psychology that behavior is often driven by unconscious influences.

In 2012 Doyen and colleagues in Brussels repeated the study with a larger sample, timing walkers with hidden infrared sensors instead of a manual stopwatch, a method prone to error and bias, and found no priming effect.
In Doyen's second experiment, walkers slowed only when the experimenters had been led to expect slower walking, suggesting experimenters' expectations helped produce the effect.

title: Word priming holds up
description: Semantic priming, in which a word makes related words quicker to recognize, is a robust finding, unlike the dramatic behavior-priming claims.

facts.text: In semantic priming, a word such as cat automatically activates related concepts such as dog, so a related word is recognized faster when it follows.
The Semantic Priming Project, from Hutchison and colleagues in 2013, is the largest database of semantic priming effects available.

title: Why minds use shortcuts
description: Heuristics save time and effort and are usually useful, but their errors are systematic, which is how researchers detect and test them.

facts.text: Tversky and Kahneman wrote in 1974 that in general heuristics are quite useful, but sometimes they lead to severe and systematic errors.
Kahneman explained that heuristics of judgment were identified by the characteristic errors they cause, and Tversky and Kahneman noted that heuristics give rise to predictable biases.

title: Harlow's cloth mother
description: Harry Harlow's infant monkeys clung to a soft cloth surrogate that gave no milk rather than a wire one that did, suggesting comfort and security, not food, anchor attachment.

facts.text: In the 1950s, Harry Harlow separated newborn monkeys from their mothers and gave each two surrogate mothers: a wire one that could give milk and a soft cloth one that gave none.
Harlow's infant monkeys spent their time clinging to the cloth mother and went to the wire mother only when they needed to feed.
Before Harlow, scientists generally thought babies become attached to whoever feeds them; Harlow concluded that comfort and security are critical to the infant-mother bond.
In Harlow's fear tests with frightening objects such as a moving toy bear, infant monkeys sought the soft cloth mother whichever surrogate fed them.
Harlow presented the cloth and wire mother findings in "The Nature of Love", his 1958 address as president of the American Psychological Association.

title: Why Harlow's studies are criticized
description: Harlow's monkey studies predate modern ethics guidelines and are now widely considered unethical and even cruel; critics call his work an ethical paradox.

facts.text: Harlow's monkey studies were performed before modern ethics guidelines, and today they are widely considered unethical and even cruel.
In a 1997 article, John Gluck described Harlow as an ethical paradox: his work showed monkeys have rich inner lives full of emotion, yet he was criticized for ignoring what his findings implied.

title: Ainsworth's Strange Situation
description: Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation stages a short separation from and reunion with a caregiver, building on Bowlby's idea of a secure base, to classify attachment.

facts.text: John Bowlby, building on Harlow's work, described attachment as a bond an infant forms with a primary caregiver, and a secure base as a caregiver whose presence lets a child explore safely.
In Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation (1970), a caregiver and infant spend time in a room with toys; a stranger enters, the caregiver leaves, then returns a few minutes later.
Ainsworth classified attachment by how infants responded to the separation and to the reunion with the caregiver.

title: Attachment styles
description: Ainsworth described secure, avoidant and resistant attachment, with disorganized added later; critics point to temperament and culture.

facts.text: Ainsworth identified three attachment types, secure, avoidant and resistant; a fourth, disorganized, was described later by Mary Main and Judith Solomon (1990).
Secure attachment is the most common type: the child uses the caregiver as a secure base, is upset when they leave and is happy when they return.
A child with avoidant attachment doesn't use the parent as a secure base, doesn't seem to care if the parent leaves and reacts to the parent much as to a stranger.
A child with resistant attachment is clingy, too fearful to explore, very upset at separation and difficult to comfort when the parent returns.
Critics note that a child's temperament may strongly influence attachment, and that attachment varies across cultures in ways Ainsworth's research didn't account for.
Comparing the United States and Japan, Fred Rothbaum and colleagues (2000) argued that attachment measures are biased toward Western values such as autonomy and exploration.

title: Piaget's stages of thinking
description: Jean Piaget proposed four stages of cognitive development (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational), each a new way of thinking.

facts.text: Jean Piaget proposed that thinking develops through four stages, sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational, each a distinct shift in how children reason.
In Piaget's sensorimotor stage, from birth to about age 2, children learn through their senses and movement and develop object permanence.
In Piaget's preoperational stage, about ages 2 to 7, children use symbols and pretend play but don't yet grasp conservation: changing something's appearance doesn't change its amount.
In Piaget's concrete operational stage, about ages 7 to 11, children think logically about real events and master conservation, such as water poured from a tall, thin glass into a short, fat one.
In Piaget's formal operational stage, from about age 11, people can reason about abstract ideas and hypothetical situations.
Piaget tested object permanence by hiding a toy under a blanket: infants who had it reached for the toy, while in his view young infants did not remember an object once it was out of sight.

title: Where later research revised Piaget
description: Looking-time studies by Renée Baillargeon and others found infants understand hidden objects months before they search for them, and many studies find milestones earlier and change more gradual than Piaget's stages.

facts.text: In Renée Baillargeon and Julie DeVos's 1991 study, 3.5-month-olds looked reliably longer when a tall carrot passing behind a screen failed to appear in the screen's window.
Infants as young as 3.5 months seem to understand that hidden objects still exist, yet they don't search for hidden objects until 7 to 8 months.
Many later studies suggest children reach cognitive milestones earlier than Piaget described, and that development is more continuous than his separate stages.

title: Theory of mind
description: Theory of mind is understanding that others have thoughts, feelings and beliefs different from your own; children develop it between about 3 and 5, at a similar age across cultures.

facts.text: Theory of mind is understanding that other people have thoughts, feelings and beliefs different from your own; children develop it between about 3 and 5 years old.
A child's theory of mind is typically marked by passing false-belief tasks, which test whether they understand that others can hold beliefs that are false.
Using one standard false-belief test in Canada, India, Peru, Samoa and Thailand, Tara Callaghan and colleagues (2005) found children passed at about age 5 in every culture.
A 2001 meta-analysis of 178 studies led by Henry Wellman found preschoolers go from below-chance to above-chance on false-belief tasks, a pattern consistent across countries.

title: The false-belief test
description: In the Sally-Anne task a child must predict that Sally will look where she left her marble, not where Anne moved it; most children pass after about age 4 to 5.

facts.text: In the Sally-Anne task, Sally puts her marble away and leaves; while she is gone, Anne moves it into her own box; the child is asked where Sally will look for her marble.
Over the age of 4 to 5, most typically developing children correctly say Sally will look where she left the marble, showing they know she holds a false belief.
In early false-belief studies, older preschoolers consistently passed while younger children systematically erred.

title: Statistical learning of words
description: Infants find words in fluent speech by tracking which sounds tend to follow which, as Saffran, Aslin and Newport showed with 8-month-olds in 1996.

facts.text: In 1996, Jenny Saffran, Richard Aslin and Elissa Newport found that 8-month-old infants could pick out words from fluent speech using only the statistics of which sounds followed which.
The infants in Saffran's study picked out the words after only 2 minutes of listening.
Finding the words in fluent, running speech is a basic task of learning a language.

title: Why early is easier for language
description: Infants start out able to hear many languages' sound differences and tune to their own; learners exposed to a language earlier reach better grammar, an advantage that fades by puberty.

facts.text: In a 1981 study led by Janet Werker, 7-month-old infants told apart two pairs of Hindi speech sounds, while English-speaking adults had trouble with the rarer pair.
Research suggests young infants can discriminate many speech sounds regardless of which language they hear at home.
Patricia Kuhl (2004) proposed that the brain's commitment to the sound patterns experienced early in life might explain why infants learn language better than adults.
In 1989, Jacqueline Johnson and Elissa Newport tested 46 Korean and Chinese speakers who had moved to the US between ages 3 and 39: the earlier they arrived, the better their English grammar.
In Johnson and Newport's study, grammar scores fell with age of arrival up to puberty; after puberty they were low, varied widely and no longer tracked arrival age.

title: Mischel's delay-of-gratification studies
description: In Walter Mischel's marshmallow studies at a Stanford preschool, children who waited longer for a bigger reward grew into more competent adolescents in his small samples.

facts.text: In the marshmallow test, a child is left alone with a treat such as a marshmallow and gets more if they wait for the adult to return instead of eating it.
Walter Mischel's delay studies used children who attended a preschool on the Stanford University campus.
In Mischel's research, 4-year-olds who delayed gratification longer grew into more competent adolescents with higher school performance.

title: The 2018 marshmallow replication
description: Watts, Duncan and Quan's 2018 replication with 918 children found the link to teen achievement half as strong and shrinking by two thirds once family background and early ability were controlled.

facts.text: Mischel and Shoda's long-term links rested on small, highly selective samples of 35 to 89 children from the Stanford community.
In 2018, Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan revisited the marshmallow test with 918 children from a larger, more diverse sample.
Among children whose mothers had not finished college, the 2018 link between waiting at 4 and achievement at 15 was half the original size.
The 2018 link shrank by about two thirds once family background, early cognitive ability and the home environment were controlled.

title: Peers and teenage risk taking
description: In experiments, adolescents take more risks with peers present, much more than adults do; this is a feature of the situation, not a sign that teens are troubled.

facts.text: Most adolescent risk taking happens in the presence of peers.
In 2005, Margo Gardner and Laurence Steinberg randomly assigned 306 people aged 13 to 16, 18 to 22, and 24 and older to do risk tasks alone or with two same-aged peers.
Gardner and Steinberg measured risk taking with "Chicken", a video driving game in which players decide whether to stop a car when a traffic light turns yellow.
People took more risks in peer groups than alone, and the peer effect was stronger for adolescents and young adults than for adults.
Most teens don't experience the extreme "storm and stress" G. Stanley Hall once suggested; only small numbers have major conflicts with parents, mostly over everyday issues like homework and chores.

title: Why watching peers raise risk
description: In Chein and colleagues' 2011 driving study, being watched by peers made adolescents, but not adults, take more risks and boosted activity in reward-related brain regions.

facts.text: In a 2011 study led by Jason Chein, adolescents playing a simulated driving game took more risks when peers watched from an adjacent room; adults did not.
When watched by peers, only the adolescents showed more activity in reward-related brain regions during fMRI scanning, and that activity predicted their later risk taking.
Chein and colleagues concluded that peers raise adolescent risk taking by heightening sensitivity to the potential reward of risky decisions.

title: Erikson's psychosocial theory
description: Erik Erikson reworked Freud's ideas into a psychosocial theory in which personality develops across the whole lifespan through eight stages, each with a task to resolve.

facts.text: Erik Erikson modified Freud's theory into a psychosocial theory stressing social interaction; where Freud believed personality is shaped only in childhood, Erikson said it develops across the lifespan.
Erikson proposed eight stages from infancy to late adulthood, each with a conflict or task to resolve; resolving it brings a sense of competence.

title: Erikson's eight life tasks
description: Erikson's tasks run from trust versus mistrust in infancy through identity in adolescence, intimacy and generativity in adulthood, to integrity versus despair in late life.

facts.text: In infancy, the task is trust versus mistrust: responsive, sensitive caregivers help a baby see the world as safe and predictable.
In adolescence, the task is identity versus role confusion, with questions like "Who am I?"
In early adulthood, the task is intimacy versus isolation; Erikson said a strong sense of self must come before intimate relationships.
In middle adulthood, the task is generativity versus stagnation: finding your life's work and contributing to others through volunteering, mentoring or raising children.
In late adulthood, the task is integrity versus despair: looking back on life with a sense of satisfaction or of failure.

title: Which abilities change with age
description: Crystallized intelligence tends to hold steady or improve with age, while fluid intelligence (processing, reasoning, memory) slows in late adulthood.

facts.text: Crystallized intelligence, the information, skills and strategies gathered through experience, tends to hold steady with age and may even improve.
In late adulthood, fluid intelligence (information processing, reasoning and memory) begins to decline, and these processes become slower.
Research has found that adults who engage in mentally stimulating activities experience less cognitive decline.

title: Emotional life in older age
description: In experience-sampling research, emotional well-being grows more positive and stable with age; socioemotional selectivity theory explains this as a shift toward emotional goals when time ahead feels shorter.

facts.text: In a study led by Laura Carstensen (2011), adults of all ages reported their emotions at five random times a day for a week, and the week was repeated 5 and 10 years later.
Aging was associated with more positive emotional well-being and greater emotional stability, even after accounting for personality, health and demographics.
Socioemotional selectivity theory holds that when time horizons shrink, emotional goals become more important than other goals; the shift comes with age, and with moves, illness or war.
With age, social networks tend to shrink in number, but the remaining friendships stay as close or closer than before.

title: Development's big questions
description: Developmental psychologists ask whether change is continuous or comes in stages, and whether development follows one course or many; stage theories say the sequence is universal, while culture shifts timing.

facts.text: Developmental psychologists ask whether change is continuous, a gradual building on existing skills, or discontinuous, coming in distinct stages.
Stage theories, such as Piaget's and Erikson's, hold that the sequence of development is universal.
Aché children in Paraguay, carried almost constantly while their mothers forage in the forest, walk at about 23 to 25 months, versus about 12 months in Western cultures.

title: Asch's conformity experiments
description: In Asch's 1950s line-judgment studies, most participants went along with a unanimous wrong answer at least once, to fit in rather than because they were unsure.

facts.text: In experiments in the 1950s, Solomon Asch asked groups to say aloud which of three lines matched a target line; only one member was a real participant, and the rest were confederates working for the researcher who, on some trials, gave an obviously wrong answer.
Asch (1955) found that 76 percent of participants, about three in four, went along with the group's wrong answer at least once.
Conformity is changing your behavior to go along with a group even if you do not agree with it; Asch's participants gave the wrong answer aloud while privately not accepting it.

Because Asch's line task was easy and unambiguous, participants did not need the group for information; they went along to fit in and avoid ridicule, which psychologists call normative social influence.

title: What raises and lowers conformity
description: Conformity rises with the size of a unanimous majority up to a point, drops sharply when one person dissents, and is lower when answers are private.

facts.text: In Asch's studies, conformity rose as the majority grew larger, but only up to a point; beyond that, adding more people did not increase it.
In Asch's research, conformity dropped sharply when at least one other group member dissented from the majority.
Conformity is more likely when answers are given publicly than when they are made privately, such as in writing, which is one reason elections use secret ballots.

title: Milgram's obedience studies
description: Milgram asked participants to give what they believed were ever stronger electric shocks; in his best-known version 65 percent went to the maximum, and obedience fell when the victim was closer or the authority weaker.

facts.text: Stanley Milgram, a social psychology professor at Yale, designed his obedience experiment to test the defense of Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann that he was just following orders.

In Milgram's 1963 study, 40 men were told they were helping with a study of learning and were asked to give a learner electric shocks for wrong answers, rising in 15-volt steps to 450 volts; the learner was a confederate who received no shocks.
When the experimenter told them to continue, 65 percent of participants in Milgram's best-known version kept going to the maximum 450 volts.

In other versions of Milgram's study, obedience fell: it dropped to 40 percent when the learner was in the same room as the teacher and fell further when the experimenter gave orders by phone; making the victim more human or the authority weaker reduced obedience.

title: What later work found about Milgram's studies
description: Archive work shows Milgram ran many versions with lower average obedience and that doubting participants obeyed more, yet a 2009 partial replication found obedience only slightly lower than his.

facts.text: A 2014 synthesis led by Nick Haslam counted 23 versions of Milgram's experiment; across the 21 comparable ones, 43.6 percent of 740 participants went to the maximum voltage.

An unpublished analysis by Milgram's assistant Taketo Murata, reported by Gina Perry and colleagues in 2020, found that in 18 of 23 versions, participants who fully believed the shocks were real gave lower shocks than those who doubted it.

In 2009 Jerry Burger published a partial replication in which 70 adults took part only up to 150 volts, the learner's first spoken protest, to protect participants; obedience was only slightly lower than in Milgram's study.

title: The Stanford prison experiment as usually told
description: In 1971 Zimbardo's team randomly assigned 24 students to be guards or prisoners in a mock prison and stopped after six days; it was taught as proof that roles make people cruel.

facts.text: In August 1971, Philip Zimbardo's team at Stanford University picked 24 healthy male college students from more than 70 volunteers and randomly assigned them to be guards or prisoners in a mock prison.
The study was planned to run for weeks but was ended after six days, with Zimbardo reporting that guards had turned abusive and prisoners showed severe distress.
The Stanford prison experiment became a famous demonstration of the claim that social roles and situations can lead ordinary people to behave cruelly.

title: Why the Stanford prison story is doubted
description: The guards were told what was expected and pushed to be tough, the archives show biased data collection, and a later study without guard guidelines turned out differently.

facts.text: At the guards' orientation, Zimbardo told them they could create fear and a sense of powerlessness in the prisoners, giving them a general sense of how he expected them to behave.
Recordings in the study's archives show the warden, an undergraduate named David Jaffe, pressing a guard to act as a 'tough guard'.

In 2018 the French researcher Thibault Le Texier published a book based on the study's archives, then a 2019 article in American Psychologist reporting that guards received precise instructions and that data collection was biased and incomplete.
Le Texier argues that Zimbardo designed the study from the outset as a demonstration of the harm prisons do, rather than as a neutral test.

In the BBC Prison Study, published in 2006 by Stephen Reicher and Alex Haslam, researchers randomly assigned men to be guards or prisoners but gave the guards no guidelines, and participants did not automatically conform to their roles.

title: The bystander effect
description: Each person is less likely to help when others are present, because responsibility feels shared; the effect is weaker in clearly dangerous emergencies, and in real conflicts someone usually helps.

facts.text: The bystander effect, described by John Darley and Bibb Latane in 1968, is the finding that a person is less likely to help someone in distress when other bystanders are present.

In Darley and Latane's 1968 study, students talking over an intercom heard another student apparently having a seizure; 85 percent of those who thought they alone heard it reported it before the fit ended, but only 31 percent of those who thought four others heard it did.
Diffusion of responsibility is the tendency for no one in a group to help because the responsibility to help is spread across everyone present.
A 2011 meta-analysis led by Peter Fischer found that the bystander effect is weaker when an emergency is seen as dangerous.

A 2020 study led by Richard Philpot of 219 real public conflicts filmed by security cameras in the UK, the Netherlands and South Africa found that in 9 of 10, at least one bystander did something to help, and more bystanders made help more likely.

title: The 38 witnesses story
description: The famous claim that 38 neighbors silently watched Kitty Genovese's murder in 1964 helped launch bystander research, but archive work found it inaccurate.

facts.text: The 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese in New York, and the story that none of her many neighbors helped, prompted research on the bystander effect.

Archive research by Rachel Manning and colleagues in 2007 found no evidence that 38 witnesses were present, that witnesses saw the murder, or that they stayed inactive; one man shouted at the attacker and a woman said she called the police.

title: The fundamental attribution error
description: People tend to explain others' behavior by their character and underestimate the situation, while explaining their own behavior by the situation.

facts.text: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to explain other people's behavior by their personality or other internal traits while underestimating the power of the situation.

Situationism holds that behavior is shaped by immediate surroundings and dispositionism that it comes from internal factors such as personality; social psychologists have tended to stress the situation and personality psychologists the person, though modern approaches weigh both.

The actor-observer bias is the classic idea (Jones and Nisbett, 1971) that people explain their own behavior more by the situation than others'; a 2006 meta-analysis of 173 studies by Bertram Malle found little overall support, with the pattern mainly for negative events.

title: Experiments on the attribution error
description: In Jones and Harris's 1967 essay study and the 1977 quizmaster study, people judged others by their behavior even when the situation plainly explained it.

facts.text: In 1967, Edward Jones and Victor Harris had Duke University students read an essay for or against Fidel Castro's Cuba; even when told a course instructor had assigned the writer's side, readers tended to judge the writer's true attitude as matching the essay.

In a 1977 quizmaster study by Lee Ross and colleagues, students randomly assigned to write and ask hard questions were rated as more knowledgeable by the contestants and by observers, who overlooked the questioners' built-in advantage.

title: Cognitive dissonance
description: Holding inconsistent beliefs and actions feels uncomfortable, so people change a behavior, change a belief or add a justification; effort can make a goal feel more valuable.

facts.text: Leon Festinger (1957) defined cognitive dissonance as the discomfort of holding inconsistent attitudes, behaviors or beliefs, such as believing smoking is harmful while smoking; people reduce it by changing a behavior, changing a belief, or adding a new justification.

In a 1959 experiment by Elliot Aronson and Judson Mills, students who went through a difficult initiation to join a deliberately dull discussion group rated it more favorably than those who had an easy initiation or none.

title: The one-dollar experiment
description: Festinger and Carlsmith (1959) paid students 1 or 20 dollars to call dull tasks fun; the 1-dollar group later rated the tasks more enjoyable because the small payment could not justify the lie.

facts.text: In Festinger and Carlsmith's 1959 experiment, students spent an hour on dull tasks, such as filling a tray with spools and turning square pegs, then were paid 1 dollar or 20 dollars to tell a waiting student the tasks were enjoyable.
Afterward, students paid 1 dollar rated the tasks as more enjoyable than students paid 20 dollars, whose ratings were close to those of a control group who told no one anything.
Festinger and Carlsmith reasoned that 20 dollars was a good enough reason to tell the lie, while 1 dollar was not, so the low-paid students reduced their dissonance by deciding the tasks were fun.

title: Two routes to persuasion
description: The elaboration likelihood model says messages persuade through a central route (thinking about the arguments) or a peripheral route (cues such as attractiveness), and central-route change lasts longer.

facts.text: Persuasion is the process of changing an attitude through some kind of communication.

The elaboration likelihood model of Richard Petty and John Cacioppo describes two routes to persuasion: a central route based on thoughtful consideration of the arguments, and a peripheral route based on cues such as a speaker's attractiveness or a celebrity endorsement.

The central route works when the audience is motivated and able to think the message through, and it tends to produce lasting attitude change, while peripheral-route change is typically less permanent.

title: Personal relevance picks the route
description: In Petty, Cacioppo and Goldman's 1981 exam study, students who would be affected were swayed by argument quality, while those who would not were swayed by the source's expertise.

facts.text: In a 1981 experiment by Petty, Cacioppo and Rachel Goldman, University of Missouri students heard a proposal for senior comprehensive exams, with strong or weak arguments, from a Princeton-chaired commission or a high school class, starting next year or in 10 years.

When the exams would start the following year, affecting the students themselves, their attitudes depended mainly on the quality of the arguments; when the exams were 10 years away, attitudes depended mainly on the source's expertise.

title: In-groups and in-group bias
description: We identify with in-groups, which feed our identity and self-esteem, and tend to prefer them over out-groups.

facts.text: An in-group is a group we identify with, and an out-group is one we see as different from us; in-group bias is a preference for our own group over other groups.
The groups we belong to are a powerful source of identity and self-esteem.

title: Tajfel's minimal group studies
description: Tajfel split schoolboys into groups on trivial or random grounds, and they still favored their own group, even choosing a bigger gap over more for everyone.

facts.text: In experiments at the University of Bristol reported in 1970, Henri Tajfel divided schoolboys aged 14 and 15 into groups on trivial grounds, such as preferring paintings by Paul Klee or Wassily Kandinsky; in fact the boys were assigned at random.
The boys then shared out points worth real money between other boys identified only by code number and group, and never to themselves.
Most boys gave more to members of their own group, and they often chose the largest difference in favor of their group even when that meant their group got less overall.
Tajfel concluded that the mere fact of being divided into groups can be enough to trigger discrimination, even with no conflict of interests and no history of hostility.

title: The WEIRD problem
description: Much psychology rests on samples from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich and Democratic societies, which are often outliers, so findings may not hold everywhere.

facts.text: In 2010, Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan argued that behavioral scientists often make broad claims about human nature from samples drawn entirely from WEIRD societies: Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich and Democratic.

Their review found substantial variation in results across populations and concluded that WEIRD participants are often outliers, among the least representative populations for generalizing about humans.
In 2008, Jeffrey Arnett showed that research in six leading APA journals focused mostly on Americans, who make up less than 5 percent of the world's population.

title: Culture shapes thinking
description: People from different cultures attend to and explain the world differently, for example in how much they notice context.

facts.text: In a 2001 study by Takahiko Masuda and Richard Nisbett, Japanese and American participants watched animated underwater scenes; the Japanese made more statements about the background and relationships in the scenes than the Americans did.

People from individualistic cultures, such as the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom, tend to commit the fundamental attribution error more than people from collectivistic cultures, which focus more on relationships and the group.

title: Following a cause, not just an order
description: Reanalyses suggest people follow authorities when they identify with the cause and believe it is right, and they tend to refuse bare commands.

facts.text: A reanalysis by Alex Haslam and Stephen Reicher reports that Milgram's participants tended to continue when prodded in the name of the experiment ('The experiment requires that you continue') but typically refused a direct order ('You have no other choice, you must go on').
Haslam and Reicher argue that people's willingness to follow authorities depends on identifying with the authority and believing it is right, rather than on blind conformity.

title: The Big Five personality traits
description: Most psychologists describe personality with five broad traits, openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism (OCEAN), found across cultures.

facts.text: In 1936 Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert found about 4,500 English dictionary words describing lasting personality traits.
The Five Factor Model, or Big Five, is the most popular theory in personality psychology; its traits spell OCEAN: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism.

Openness covers imagination, feelings and ideas; conscientiousness, self-discipline and achievement-striving; extraversion, sociability and assertiveness; agreeableness, being cooperative and good-natured; neuroticism, a tendency to feel negative emotions.
In a 2005 study led by Robert McCrae, students in 50 cultures rated someone they knew well, and the five-factor structure was recognizable in all 50.

title: Traits as dials, measured by self-report
description: Each Big Five trait runs along a spectrum on which most people sit midway, and traits are usually measured with self-report inventories that people can answer to look good.

facts.text: Everyone has each Big Five trait; each runs along a spectrum, and most people sit somewhere midway rather than at either end.
Personality is often measured with self-report inventories: statements rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), which people may answer in ways that look good.

title: Personality type tests like the Myers-Briggs
description: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator sorts people into 16 types from four either-or preferences, though most people score between the extremes.

facts.text: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator was developed by Isabel Briggs Myers and her mother, Katharine Briggs, after Katharine read Carl Jung's work on psychological types.
The Myers-Briggs asks about four pairs of opposite preferences, such as extraversion versus introversion, and combines them into one of 16 types.
On the Myers-Briggs scales most people score between the two extremes, and cut-off points split each scale, so people with close scores can get opposite letters.
A 1989 study by Robert McCrae and Paul Costa found no support for truly either-or Myers-Briggs preferences, though its four scales tracked four of the Big Five.

title: Reliability of personality tests
description: A reliable test gives the same result each time; as many as half of people get a new Myers-Briggs type on retest, while Big Five scores stay closely matched.

facts.text: A test's reliability is its consistency: a reliable test gives the same result each time it measures the same thing.
In a 1993 review, David Pittenger reported that as many as 50 percent of people get a different Myers-Briggs type when retested only five weeks later.
Retest scores on the NEO PI-R, a widely used Big Five questionnaire, stay closely matched over weeks and even years.

title: How personality matures with age
description: Personality is partly heritable, yet on average people become more conscientious, emotionally stable and socially confident, especially between 20 and 40.

facts.text: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart, run from 1979 to 1999, found that identical twins have very similar personalities whether raised together or apart.

A 2006 review by Brent Roberts and colleagues of 92 samples found people grow more conscientious, emotionally stable and socially dominant (assertive), especially from 20 to 40; agreeableness changed only in old age.

title: Rank-order stability of personality
description: How consistently people keep their rank on a trait relative to others rises from childhood and levels off between ages 50 and 70.

facts.text: A 2000 review by Brent Roberts and Wendy DelVecchio found that people's rank on traits grows more consistent from childhood through the college years and age 30, leveling off between 50 and 70.

title: What IQ tests measure and predict
description: IQ tests began with Binet and Simon in 1905, score abilities like verbal comprehension and working memory against an average of 100, and predict grades only partly.

facts.text: In 1905 Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon in France published the first practical intelligence test, designed to identify schoolchildren who needed extra educational help.

Modern IQ tests such as the Wechsler scales give scores for areas like verbal comprehension, working memory and processing speed, combined into an overall score; on most IQ tests the average is set at 100.
IQ tests are periodically recalibrated against new groups of test takers so the average stays at 100.

A 1996 American Psychological Association report led by Ulric Neisser found IQ explains only about a quarter of the differences in school grades; persistence, interest and willingness to study matter too.

title: The Flynn effect
description: Average IQ scores rose about three points per decade in the 20th century, too fast and too clearly within families to be explained by genes.

facts.text: Average IQ scores rose about three points per decade across the 20th century, a rise called the Flynn effect after James Flynn.
A 2018 study of Norwegian men found the Flynn effect's rise and later decline among brothers in the same families, pointing to environmental causes rather than genes.
Proposed causes of the Flynn effect include better nutrition, more schooling and a more complex environment; the question remains unresolved.

title: Stress as appraisal
description: Stress depends on how a person appraises an event (primary appraisal of threat or challenge) and their resources to cope (secondary appraisal).

facts.text: In Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman's view, stress is a process in which people respond to events they appraise as overwhelming or threatening.
A primary appraisal judges how much harm or threat an event holds, seeing it as a threat or a challenge; a secondary appraisal judges the options to cope and how well they'd work.
People feel stress when they appraise an event as harmful and believe its demands exceed their resources to handle it.
Eustress is good stress that motivates performance; distress is stress so excessive that performance declines.

title: Changing appraisal changes the stress response
description: In a 1964 experiment, the same stressful film raised or lowered viewers' bodily stress depending on the soundtrack's framing.

facts.text: In a 1964 study led by Joseph Speisman with Richard Lazarus, a stressful film with a threat-stressing soundtrack raised viewers' skin conductance, a bodily sign of stress, while calmer soundtracks lowered it.

title: Problem-focused and emotion-focused coping
description: Coping is the effort to deal with stress, either by changing the problem or by reducing the emotions it brings; people lean on each depending on how controllable a stressor seems.

facts.text: Coping means the mental and behavioral efforts people use to deal with problems relating to stress.
Problem-focused coping tries to manage or change the problem, like getting tutoring; emotion-focused coping tries to reduce the negative emotions, like watching a comedy.
Many stressors draw both kinds of coping, but problem-focused coping is more likely with stressors seen as controllable, and emotion-focused with ones people feel powerless to change.

title: The goodness-of-fit idea in coping
description: Coping may work best when it fits how controllable a stressor is; daily studies support this, though other tests give only partial support.

facts.text: In a 2004 study, 190 students reported their most stressful event each day for 28 days; problem-focused coping went with better mood more strongly when the stressor was controllable.
The goodness-of-fit hypothesis, from Lazarus and Folkman, says coping works best when it matches how controllable a stressor is; tests have found only partial support.

title: Resilience is common
description: Resilience, keeping stable healthy functioning after loss or potential trauma, differs from recovery and is more common than once believed.

facts.text: George Bonanno (2004) separated recovery, in which functioning drops for months or longer before returning, from resilience, keeping relatively stable, healthy functioning.
Resilient people may still have brief disruptions, such as several weeks of restless sleep, but keep a stable path of healthy functioning.
Research shows resilience after loss or potential trauma is common rather than rare, and it is not a sign of pathology.
In a 2006 study led by Bonanno of 2,752 New York-area residents after the September 11 attacks, about 65 percent were resilient, and never less than a third of any group.

title: The myth that absent grief is unhealthy
description: Experts once believed little grief signaled denial and delayed grief; a prospective study found many calm bereaved people were genuinely resilient.

facts.text: In a 1993 survey, 65 percent of self-identified bereavement experts said absent grief usually stems from denial and is harmful in the long run.
Most bereavement studies begin after the death has occurred, so they can't show what people were like beforehand.
In a prospective study with data from about three years before a spouse died, about 46 percent had low depression before and 18 months after, and weren't cold or distant.
Studies following bereaved people found no clear evidence of delayed grief, and most resilient people still felt some yearning and pangs.

title: Hedonic adaptation
description: People get used to good and bad changes, so their emotional impact fades, though adaptation to some events is incomplete.

facts.text: In 1978, Philip Brickman and colleagues found 22 major lottery winners were not happier than 22 comparison people and took less pleasure from everyday events.
Brickman's team proposed two forces: contrast, as the thrill of winning makes ordinary pleasures feel smaller, and habituation, as new pleasures lose their value.
Hedonic adaptation is the fading over time of the joys and sorrows that follow good and bad events.
A 2007 review by Richard Lucas found divorce, a spouse's death, unemployment and disability are linked to lasting changes in wellbeing, and people differ in how fully they adapt.

title: Relationships and happiness
description: The happiest people in a 2002 study stood out for strong social relationships rather than more good events; good relationships were necessary but not sufficient.

facts.text: In 2002, Ed Diener and Martin Seligman compared the happiest 10 percent of 222 students with average and very unhappy students; the happiest had stronger social relationships and were more extraverted, but did not have more good events.
In Diener and Seligman's study, good social relationships were necessary for high happiness but not enough on their own.
Diener and Seligman identified the happiest students by combining peer reports with the students' own self-reports, gathered over months and daily for 51 days.

title: Habits and their context
description: Many daily behaviors repeat in the same setting, and habits are easier to change when that context is disrupted, as after a move.

facts.text: In 2002 diary studies led by Wendy Wood, between a third and a half of students' behaviors (35 percent in one study, 43 percent in the other) were done almost daily in the same place, often while thinking about something else.
In a 2016 field experiment in Peterborough, England, a push toward greener habits worked better on people who had moved house within about three months, while old habits were disrupted.

title: If-then plans
description: Implementation intentions spell out when, where and how to act in if-then form, and they reliably help people reach goals.

facts.text: An implementation intention, or if-then plan, spells out when, where and how you'll act: 'If situation Y happens, then I'll do X.' A goal alone doesn't guarantee action.
In 2006, Peter Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran pooled 94 tests with more than 8,000 people; if-then plans had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
If-then plans helped people get started on goals and shield them from unwanted distractions.

title: Personality predicts life outcomes
description: In long-term studies, personality traits predicted death rates, divorce and career attainment about as well as socioeconomic status and cognitive ability.

facts.text: A 2007 review by Brent Roberts and colleagues found traits predicted mortality, divorce and job attainment about as well as socioeconomic status and cognitive ability.
That review counted only prospective studies, which follow people over time, and tried to limit itself to studies that controlled for background factors.

title: What makes something a mental disorder
description: A mental disorder is a clinically significant disturbance in thinking, emotion regulation or behavior, usually with distress or problems functioning; being unusual, or an expected reaction such as grief, is not enough.

facts.text: In 2023 nearly 1 in 7 people worldwide, about 1.2 billion, were living with a mental disorder; anxiety and depressive disorders were the most common.
A mental disorder is characterized by a clinically significant disturbance in a person's cognition, emotional regulation or behavior.
Mental illnesses are health conditions involving changes in emotion, thinking or behavior, associated with distress and/or problems functioning in social, work or family activities.

Being atypical is not enough to count as a disorder (red hair is uncommon but not a disorder), and expected or culturally approved responses to events, such as sadness after a loved one's death, are not disorders.

title: The DSM and the ICD
description: US clinicians classify mental disorders with the American Psychiatric Association's DSM (first edition 1952, current DSM-5-TR from 2022), whose criteria say which symptoms must be present and for how long; much of the world uses the WHO's ICD.

facts.text: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), published by the American Psychiatric Association, is the main system US mental health professionals use to classify disorders; its first edition appeared in 1952 and the current version, DSM-5-TR, in 2022.
DSM criteria specify which symptoms must be present, and for how long, for a diagnosis, and the manual is used by psychiatrists, psychologists, counselors and other health professionals.
The World Health Organization publishes the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), which is more often used for clinical diagnosis around the world.

title: How evidence moved the line
description: The first DSM listed homosexuality as a disorder; after research such as Evelyn Hooker's found no more disturbance in gay men, the American Psychiatric Association removed it in 1973, reasoning that disorders involve distress or impairment.

facts.text: In the late 1950s the psychologist Evelyn Hooker compared gay and heterosexual men who were not psychiatric patients and found no more signs of psychological disturbance in the gay men.

The first DSM (1952) classified homosexuality as a disorder; in 1973 the American Psychiatric Association concluded that disorders regularly cause distress or impairment and homosexuality itself does not, and voted to remove it.

title: Everyday anxiety versus an anxiety disorder
description: Anxiety is normal and useful, but in an anxiety disorder it does not go away, can get worse and gets in the way of work, school and relationships.

facts.text: Feeling anxious is a normal part of life, and anxiety can be useful: it motivates people to take actions that head off future problems.
In anxiety disorders, anxiety does not go away, is felt in many situations and can get worse over time, and symptoms can interfere with job performance, schoolwork and relationships.
NIMH advises talking to a health care provider if anxiety starts to cause problems in everyday life, such as at school, at work or with friends and family.

title: Panic attacks and panic disorder
description: A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes; panic disorder means repeated unexpected attacks plus ongoing worry about more, and many people have an isolated attack without the disorder.

facts.text: A panic attack is a period of intense fear or discomfort that develops abruptly and peaks within minutes, with symptoms such as a racing heart, sweating and trembling.
Panic disorder involves frequent, unexpected panic attacks plus ongoing worry about future attacks or changes in behavior, such as avoiding places where attacks happened.
In a large US survey led by Ronald Kessler (2006), about 23 percent of Americans had had isolated panic attacks in their lives without meeting the criteria for panic disorder.

title: Specific phobias
description: A specific phobia is strong, lasting fear of one object or situation, out of proportion to the real danger, that leads people to avoid it.

facts.text: A specific phobia is excessive, distressing and persistent fear of a particular object or situation that is out of proportion to the actual threat, and people often go to great lengths to avoid it.

title: Depression is not the same as sadness
description: Sadness usually passes; depression (major depressive disorder) brings severe symptoms most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, affecting how a person feels, thinks and manages daily life.

facts.text: Everyone feels sad or low sometimes, and these feelings usually pass; depression, also called major depressive disorder, is different, with severe symptoms that affect how a person feels, thinks and handles daily activities such as sleeping, eating or working.
To be diagnosed with depression, a person must have symptoms most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks.

title: Why no single cause explains depression
description: Genes, biology, environment and psychological factors combine in depression; the 'chemical imbalance' or low-serotonin story is too simple, twin studies put heritability near 37 percent, and antidepressants still help many people.

facts.text: Research suggests that genetic, biological, environmental and psychological factors all play a role in depression.

It is often said that depression results from a chemical imbalance, but that figure of speech doesn't capture how complex the condition is; faulty mood regulation, genetic vulnerability and stressful life events all contribute.

A 2022 review led by Joanna Moncrieff found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by lowered serotonin; other researchers disputed its methods and noted the serotonin theory never claimed a single-chemical imbalance.
A 2000 review of twin studies by Patrick Sullivan and colleagues estimated the heritability of major depression at about 37 percent.
A 2018 analysis led by Andrea Cipriani, pooling 522 trials, found that all 21 antidepressants studied worked better than placebo for adults with major depression.
Decisions about antidepressants, with or without talk therapy, are made by the person with depression together with their treating doctor.

title: ADHD, bipolar disorder and PTSD in brief
description: ADHD is frequent, interfering inattention, hyperactivity or impulsivity; bipolar disorder brings clear shifts between manic and depressive episodes; PTSD can follow trauma, though most people who go through trauma recover.

facts.text: ADHD involves inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity; it is common for people to show these behaviors sometimes, but in ADHD they are frequent, occur across situations and interfere with daily life, and symptoms usually continue from childhood into adulthood.

Bipolar disorder causes clear shifts in a person's mood, energy, activity levels and concentration, with manic episodes of extremely 'up', elated, irritable or energized behavior and depressive episodes of very 'down' periods.

PTSD may be diagnosed when symptoms last for an extended period after a traumatic event and interfere with daily life; people with PTSD may keep feeling stressed or frightened even when they are not in danger.

Many people have reactions such as anxiety or trouble sleeping after a traumatic event, but most recover as their reactions lessen over time, and not everyone who lives through a dangerous event develops PTSD.

title: Why casual labels like "so OCD" mislead
description: OCD means unwanted, anxiety-causing obsessions and compulsions that bring no pleasure, only brief relief, and can take over an hour a day, which is very different from simply liking things neat.

facts.text: In OCD, obsessions are intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges or mental images that make most people anxious, and compulsions are repetitive behaviors a person feels the urge to do, often in response to an obsession.

People with OCD don't get pleasure from their compulsions, only temporary relief from anxiety; they may spend more than 1 hour a day on obsessions or compulsions and can't control them even when they know they're excessive.

title: Cognitive behavioral therapy
description: CBT, growing from Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy of the early 1960s, helps people spot and question unhelpful thoughts and change how they act, focusing on current problems over a limited number of sessions.

facts.text: The psychiatrist Aaron Beck studied psychoanalysis early in his career, came to believe it lacked scientific rigor and evidence, and in the early 1960s developed cognitive therapy, helping patients identify 'automatic' negative thoughts that contribute to depression.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a talking therapy in which a therapist helps a person change how they think and act; it treats thoughts, feelings, physical sensations and actions as linked and questions unhelpful thoughts and beliefs.

CBT focuses on current problems rather than the past, and most people have between 5 and 15 sessions; it is used for depression, anxiety, OCD and PTSD among other conditions, but it may not work for everyone, and other treatments are available.

title: How we know therapy works
description: Smith and Glass's 1977 analysis of 375 studies found the average person in therapy better off than 75 percent of untreated people, with few differences among types of therapy.

facts.text: In 1977 Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass combined 375 controlled studies of therapy and found that the average person who received therapy was better off than 75 percent of untreated people.
Smith and Glass found few important differences in effectiveness among quite different types of therapy.

title: Stigma and respectful language
description: Stigma (public, self and structural) makes people reluctant to seek or stay in treatment; person-first language, dropping casual 'crazy', and saying 'died by suicide' instead of 'committed suicide' reduce it.

facts.text: Stigma about mental illness takes three forms: public stigma (negative attitudes others hold), self-stigma (internalized shame about one's own condition) and structural stigma (policies that limit opportunities).
Stigma leads to reluctance to seek help or treatment and a reduced likelihood of staying with treatment.

Person-first language puts the focus on the individual rather than the diagnosis, for example 'a person with schizophrenia' rather than 'a schizophrenic', and casual use of words like 'crazy' perpetuates harmful stereotypes.
NIMH advises avoiding terms such as 'committing suicide', 'successful suicide' or 'failed suicide'; mental health groups recommend saying 'died by suicide' instead.

title: Where to point someone who needs help
description: Asking someone directly about suicide does not increase suicidal thoughts and can identify risk; in the US, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline offers free, confidential support by call or text.

facts.text: Asking someone directly whether they are thinking about suicide can be the best way to identify someone at risk, and studies show that asking does not increase suicidal thoughts.

In the United States, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, launched in July 2022, offers free, confidential support 24 hours a day by calling or texting 988, for anyone in suicidal crisis or emotional distress.

title: The replication crisis
description: When the Open Science Collaboration repeated 100 psychology studies in 2015, only about a third found the result again, and effects averaged about half their original size.

facts.text: In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration reported repeating 100 studies from three psychology journals: 97 percent of the originals had statistically significant results, but only 36 percent of the repeats did, and effects averaged about half their original size.

title: How false findings got into print
description: Undisclosed flexibility in collecting, analyzing and reporting data, shown by the 2011 'When I'm Sixty-Four' demonstration, plus small studies, selective reporting and publication bias let false findings through.

facts.text: In 2011 Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn showed that undisclosed flexibility in collecting, analyzing and reporting data, such as when to stop collecting or which measures to report, can make almost anything look significant.

Using such flexible choices, Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn 'found' that listening to the Beatles song 'When I'm Sixty-Four' made people nearly a year and a half younger, a deliberately impossible result.

title: How psychology changed after the crisis
description: In a Registered Report a journal reviews and accepts a study's plan before any data exist, removing the reward for small samples, selective reporting and publication bias; the format began around 2013 and over 300 journals offer it.

facts.text: In a Registered Report, a journal peer-reviews a study's plan before data are collected and accepts it in principle whatever the results; the format targets low statistical power, selective reporting of results and publication bias (favoring positive results).
Registered Reports began around 2013 at the journal Cortex, and over 300 journals now offer them.

title: How power posing spread
description: A 2010 study of 42 people by Carney, Cuddy and Yap reported that one-minute expansive poses raised felt power, testosterone and risk taking; Amy Cuddy's 2012 TED talk made the idea famous.

facts.text: In a 2010 study, Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap had 42 participants hold expansive 'high-power' or closed 'low-power' poses for one minute each, and reported that high-power poses raised feelings of power, testosterone and risk taking and lowered cortisol.
Amy Cuddy's 2012 TED talk on power posing became one of the most watched TED talks ever.

title: What replications showed about power posing
description: Ranehill's 2015 replication with 200 people found no hormone or risk-taking effects, lead author Carney disowned the effect in 2016, and only a small, debated effect on how powerful people say they feel remains.

facts.text: In 2015 Eva Ranehill and colleagues tested power posing with 200 participants and found no effect on hormones or risk taking, though participants reported feeling more powerful.
In 2016 Dana Carney, the original lead author, wrote 'I do not believe that "power pose" effects are real', calling the original sample size tiny and the data flimsy.
Carney wrote that the original self-report measure of feeling powerful was p-hacked: many different power questions were asked and the ones that 'worked' were reported.

Later large analyses found an effect of posture on how powerful people say they feel, while hormone and behavior effects are largely unsupported; how much the felt-power effect means is still debated.

title: The learning-styles myth
description: People readily name a preferred learning style, but a 2008 review found virtually no evidence that matching teaching to it improves learning.

facts.text: The learning-styles idea holds that people learn best when teaching matches their preferred mode, for example visual presentation for a 'visual learner' (the meshing hypothesis); it is widespread in education from kindergarten to graduate school.

A 2008 review by Harold Pashler and colleagues found ample evidence that people will state preferences for how information is presented, but virtually no evidence that matching teaching to those preferences improves learning.

Of the few studies able to test learning styles properly, several flatly contradicted matching, and Pashler's review advised spending limited education resources on practices with a strong evidence base instead.

title: Why venting anger backfires
description: The idea that venting releases anger comes from Breuer and Freud's catharsis, but Bushman's 2002 punching-bag study found venting while dwelling on the provoker increased anger and aggression.

facts.text: The idea that venting drains anger traces to catharsis: Josef Breuer and Sigmund Freud held that expressing pent-up emotion was better than bottling it up, the basis of the 'hydraulic' model of anger.

In a 2002 study by Brad Bushman, angered people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who angered them felt angrier and were more aggressive than people who did nothing; doing nothing worked better than venting.
